triage.summary: The watchErrorStream function converts upstream errors into simple strings instead of wrapping them, breaking use of errors.Is and errors.As for error inspection.

evidence.text:
`watchErrorStream` doesn't wrap the upstream error
### What happened?

`watchErrorStream` function doesn't wrap the upstream error emitted during reading from the websocket, instead it transforms the error into a simple string making it impossible to use errors.Is/As with the underlying error

```
func watchErrorStream(errorStream io.Reader, d errorStreamDecoder) chan error {
	errorChan := make(chan error)

	go func() {
		defer runtime.HandleCrash()

		message, err := io.ReadAll(errorStream)
		switch {
		case err != nil && err != io.EOF:
			errorChan <- fmt.Errorf("error reading from error stream: %s", err)
		case len(message) > 0:
			errorChan <- d.decode(message)
		default:
			errorChan <- nil
		}
		close(errorChan)
	}()

	return errorChan
}

```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/42c4ddbe2d8efe95481d10ccfc9ca098a71e83e9/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/remotecommand/errorstream.go#L31-L54

### What did you expect to happen?

`watchErrorStream` should wrap the underlying error so clients can inspect using `errors.As/Is` instead of transforming the error into a string.

TITLE: Watch of a single namespace using /api/v1/watch/namespaces/$name missing all events in 1.27+
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We upgraded our test cluster to `1.28.8` (GKE `1.28.8-gke.1095000`) and noticed that some of our tests began to time out when watching for events that never arrived. 

Upon investigation, it appears that there is a regression in the deprecated path-based watch API for at least `namespaces` e.g. `http://localhost:8001/api/v1/watch/namespaces/<name>`. We have not been able to reproduce this with any other resource type.

When creating a watch for a namespace (see `how to reproduce`) we see the initial `added` event, but then we do not see subsequent events if we modify the namespace e.g. add a label or annotation. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect to see events when the namespace is altered. E.g. adding a label should produce a `MODIFIED` event with the contents.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a new test namespace e.g. `kubectl create namespace test-namespace`
2. Create a proxy to the master `kubectl proxy`
3. Curl the watch path of the namespace that has been created e.g. `http://localhost:8001/api/v1/watch/namespaces/test-namespace`
4. In another shell, modify the namespace to add a lab
ROOT CAUSE: The watch request for a single namespace was incorrectly scoped by setting a non-empty namespace in the watch cache, whereas events were dispatched with an empty namespace. This mismatch meant events were never delivered to watchers using the deprecated path-based watch API for namespaces.
FIX: kube-apiserver: fixes a 1.27+ regression watching a single namespace via the deprecated /api/v1/watch/namespaces/$name endpoint where watch events were not delivered after the watch was established
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go, test/integration/apimachinery/watch_namespace_test.go

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. This leads to users receiving misleading or incorrect URLs without an obvious indication that an earlier error occurred during request construction.
FIX: client-go: add an Error() function on Request
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request_test.go

TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cache_watcher_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher_whitebox_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ready_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the function `watchErrorStream` converts an upstream error from `io.ReadAll` into a simple formatted string error using fmt.Errorf without wrapping the original error. This stripping of the error context prevents downstream clients from using Go's `errors.Is` or `errors.As` to inspect or check the original error type or value.

TITLE: During the deployment of Kubernetes 1.31.0 and MultiCIDRServiceAllocator was enabled, which then led to a failure when creating a service.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When deploying Kubernetes 1.31.0 with MultiCIDRServiceAllocator enabled, an error occurs when trying to create a service in the cluster with the following error message:

```bash
root@controller-node-1:~# kubectl apply -f test-service.yaml
Error from server (InternalError): error when creating "test-service.yaml": Internal error occurred: failed to allocate a serviceIP: range is full
```

Am I missing some necessary configuration? Can you help me take a look?  Thanks.

### What did you expect to happen?

Can successfully create a service

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy k8s and enable the featureGate MultiCIDRServiceAllocator function
2. Then create a service and enable IPv6
3. The service yaml information for the test is as follows:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: dual-stack-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
    - IPv6
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
```

4. Disable MultiCIDRServiceAllocator fe
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the secondary IP range used by the legacy allocator was incorrectly initialized with the primary range's value. This mismatch caused allocation failures in the legacy allocator when services requested IPs from the secondary range, resulting in the system mistakenly reporting that the IP range was full, even though it was not.
FIX: fix a bug with dual stack clusters using the beta feature MultiCIDRServiceAllocator can not create dual stack Services or Services with IPs on the secondary range. User that want to use this feature in 1.30 with dual stack clusters can workaround the issue by setting the feature gate DisableAllocatorDualWrite to true
FILES: pkg/registry/core/rest/storage_core.go, test/integration/dualstack/dualstack_test.go

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The control plane comes up just fine but then when you try to create a k8s service, it fails due to a broken behavior with the IP Allocator

```
Since this is not really a supported version of the k8s, I went around digging up a bit more to see what is the regular behavior and found this to be very inconsistent across a few release branches.

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the IP allocator code uses big.Int to represent IP addresses for arithmetic. TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger
FILES: plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/testdata/cluster-roles.yaml

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the IPv6 service IP allocator supports CIDRs larger than /112 (e.g., /108) but is internally limited to managing a maximum of 64k addresses corresponding to a /112 range. Due to the dual allocator mode enabled by the feature gate, the allocator's logic wrongly selects IPv6 addresses that are outside the permissible /112 bitmap range, causing the legacy allocator check to fail allocation and report the address range as full, even though it is not. This mismatch arises because the new allocator does not first validate IPs against the old allocator's limitations before confirming allocations, causing invalid IP allocations and consequent failures.

claims.text: The ticket description and investigation reveal that the Kubernetes IP allocator for services allocates IPv6 addresses using a bitmap capped at a /112 range, although larger CIDRs such as /108 are configured, causing allocation failures when the dual allocator feature gate is enabled.

The code in ipallocator.go for allocateNextService tries to allocate a service IP address from the upper range first, then falls back to the lower range, but does not ensure that the address chosen by the new allocator is valid according to the legacy allocator's capped bitmap size, which leads to allocation rejection.

As per the detailed explanation in the ticket, the dual allocator logic should check the old allocator first and confirm writes in the new allocator in order to maintain consistency, but the current implementation mistakenly allows the new allocator to pick an out-of-range IP that the old allocator rejects, causing allocation to fail with 'range is full'.

Past Kubernetes issues (kb-127588) describe related bugs where dual-stack IP allocator mismatches cause erroneous 'range is full' errors, especially when feature gates for dual write mode are involved, illustrating the underlying design and synchronization challenges between allocators.

TITLE: CRD validation allows invalid CABundles that will fail setting up handlers
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A CRDs with an invalid conversion webhook CABundle failed to serve requests not requiring conversion.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since creating cr-1.yaml doesn't require conversion, I would have expected either:

1. An error response when attempting to create/update the CRD with an invalid CABundle
2. Only an error when conversion is required to server a request

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Create a mult-version CRD with a conversion webhook configured with an invalid CABundle:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: replicant.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                myfield:
                  type: integer
    - name: v2
      served: true
      storage: false
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              ty
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the CRD validation logic allowed invalid or non-PEM-encoded CABundles to be accepted when creating or updating CustomResourceDefinitions. This caused failures later when setting up conversion webhook handlers, which expect a valid CA certificate bundle for secure communication. Without proper validation at CRD creation time, invalid CABundles lead to internal errors and prevented serving requests properly.

TITLE: CEL estimated cost treats enums as strings of unbounded length
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

@robscott pointed out to me that a CEL x-kubernetes-validations rule in a CRD was hitting the estimated cost limit when performing a simple "string has prefix" check on an en enum field.

Putting a `maxLength` limit in the OpenAPI of the enum string field fixed the problem, but having to add a limit like this is counter-intuitive and unnecessary, since the allowed enum values already make the max allowed length obvious.

### What did you expect to happen?

The apiserver automatically computes the max length of an enum as the length of the longest allowed enum value. 

I believe we already refuse evaluate CEL rules on values that fail OpenAPI value validation, since we rely in the value validations to establish all length limits.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I haven't tested it locally, but something like this should work (given enough nested arrays):

```
openAPIV3Schema:
  type: object
  properties:
    spec:
      type: array
      items:
        type: array
        nested:
          type: string
          enum: ["low", "medium", "high"]
          x-kubernetes-validations:
            - rul
ROOT CAUSE: The cost estimation logic for CEL validation expressions treated enum string fields as having unbounded length because it did not account for the inherent length limits defined by the enum values. Without setting the maxLength to the longest enum value, the cost estimator assumed maximum length was unbounded, causing higher-than-necessary costs and limits to be hit unexpectedly.
FIX: CEL cost estimator no longer treats enums as unbounded strings when determining its length. Instead, the length is set to the longest possible enum value.

TITLE: CEL stored messageExpressions of CRDs are not validated with the correct CEL environment
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Noticed a copy & paste issue when reading through the CEL code.

Basically here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/validation/validation.go#L182

This should be 
> expressions.messageExpressions.Insert(v.MessageExpression)
instead of:
> expressions.messageExpressions.Insert(v.Rule)

The impact of this issue should be that messageExpressions are always evaluated with the CEL environment of the compatibility version. But stored (i.e. pre-existing) messageExpressions should be evaluated with a CEL environment with the "max" version instead.

For users of Kubernetes this means that messageExpressions deployed with one minor version of Kubernetes might not work anymore if they rollback e.g. by one minor version.



### What did you expect to happen?

messageExpressions should be treated the same way as rules in that regard.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Deploy Kubernetes 1.30
* Deploy CRD that uses messageExpression that is using Sets (which became available with Kubernetes 1.30 that is using compatibilty version 1.29)
* 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the stored messageExpressions for CRDs were inserted incorrectly using the environment intended for rules rather than being inserted and validated with the correct, up-to-date CEL environment. This caused messageExpressions deployed with a newer Kubernetes version to be validated with an outdated compatibility environment, breaking compatibility on rollback scenarios.
FIX: Validate CRD stored messageExpressions with the correct CEL environment

TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready

TITLE: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-i
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the initial list result in the Reflector retains references to a large slice of objects, and if any object pointer from that slice is still in use, the Go runtime keeps the entire backing array in memory. This happens because the ObjectList contains a slice of objects (not pointers), and the Reflector takes pointers to these objects, preventing garbage collection of the initial slice. Thus, memory is not freed even when most objects are deleted or changed, leading to high memory consumption.
FIX: client-go: Improved memory use of reflector caches when watching large numbers of objects which do not change frequently

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

TITLE: High cpu usage in json.compact call
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I was debugging performance of case with heavy watch traffic of CRD objects and found interesting suboptimality: we burn significant amount of CPU on json.compact calls that deserialize JSONs to validate correctness of already serialized objects: 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/169510517-e5b23c43-b15c-4f6d-adf1-cf36ccf6e203.png)

It looks like while in WatchServer.ServeHTTP we manage to reuse serialized objects (cachingObject) in object serialization: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L247-L251, we then wrap this objects in metav1.Event object and serialize it again: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L271

While that object consists of single enum and already serialized raw object it is expected that its serialization will be cheap. And it is for protobufs where we simply copy bytes:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that although the system reuses already serialized JSON objects to avoid redundant serialization, wrapping these objects inside event wrappers triggers repeated JSON compaction and validation in each watch client. This unnecessary JSON deserialization and re-validation incurs high CPU usage as each watcher separately compacts the JSON despite the data being previously serialized and valid.
FIX: Refactor streaming watch encoder to enable caching
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/response.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/response_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go, test/integration/apiserver/apiserver_test.go

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Initially observed gradual, linear growth in kube-apiserver's working set size (`container_memory_working_set_bytes`) over the course of a week in an OpenShift 4.13.0-rc.2 (downstream of Kubernetes v1.26.2) cluster that could not be reproduced on OpenShift 4.12.0 (Kubernetes v1.25.4).

A heap profile shows:

```

Time: Apr 12, 2023 at 12:41pm (EDT)
Active filters:
   focus=APIServiceRegistrationController
Showing nodes accounting for 193MB, 15.97% of 1208.72MB total
Dropped 4 nodes (cum <= 6.04MB)
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
         0     0%     0%   194.01MB 16.05%  k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.BackoffUntil
         0     0%     0%   194.01MB 16.05%  k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.BackoffUntil.func1

ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by incorrect use of the client-go TLS transport cache when a custom dialer was used. The APIServiceRegistrationController's sync process repeatedly created new TLS configurations and client transports without properly leveraging the caching mechanism, leading to an unbounded accumulation of transport objects and thus a memory leak in the kube-apiserver process.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the watch cache interval code redundantly recomputes labels and fields for every cached object by calling getAttrsFunc(elem.Object) even though these attributes have already been computed and stored in the storeElement's Labels and Fields fields. This unnecessary recomputation triggers significant temporary memory allocations for all objects during watch cache interval generation, driving high memory usage especially with large numbers of small objects.

claims.text: The high temporary memory usage during watch cache interval generation is caused by repeated calls to getAttrsFunc on each object in the cache, even though labels and fields are already stored in the object (storeElement.Labels and storeElement.Fields). This redundant computation causes excessive allocations.
An optimization proposed in the ticket to reuse the cached labels and fields in storeElement instead of recalculating them significantly reduces temporary memory usage, confirming the root cause.

triage.summary: Sidecar containers defined as initContainers with restartPolicy Always are not accessible via Service endpoints, resulting in connection refused despite pod ports being available.

evidence.text:
Sidecar Containers for Services are not accessible
### What happened?

I'm using a helm chart to deploy an application, and I typically insert an specific proxy I need as a legacy sidecar (after init). However, this helm chart specifically does now allow specifying additional containers (again, legacy sidecar pattern), but it does allow specifying init containers using the newer [Sidecar Containers](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/) feature.

The sidecar config might look like this with the new sidecar pattern:
```yaml
      initContainers:
        - name: myproxy
          image: myproxy
          restartPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: proxy-port
              protocol: TCP
```

After deploying this:
- The `v1/Service` has endpoints that point to the target pods
- Manually, I can connect to `<pod IP>:8080`
- Attempting to connect to the service results in a connection refused.

### What did you expect to happen?

The connection to the sidecar should work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a pod with a named port in a container under `initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always`
- Create a `v1/Service` that has a `selector` that targets the pod
- Attempt to lookup the SRV record

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
Client Version: v1.31.0
Kustomize Version: v5.4.2
Server Version: v1.30.5-

TITLE: Named ports specified in sidecar container pod spec are not available to services
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When migrating a sidecar container to a native sidecar container (initContainer with restartPolicy=Always), traffic going via the Kubernetes Service did not reach the application container/sidecar container.

### What did you expect to happen?

The traffic should have reached the sidecar container like before the migration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Pod with a native sidecar container (initContainer) with a named port, as well as a Kubernetes Service using that named port as its targetPort. This port is not listed in the Endpoint.

Apply the following:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sidecar-ports
  labels:
    app: sidecar-ports
spec:
  containers:
  - image: bloomberg/goldpinger:3.10.1
    name: goldpinger
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
  initContainers:
  # note: no envoy configuration is provided, the steps to reproduce involve reading other Kubernetes manifests (Endpoints)
  - image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.73.7
    name: tls-terminator
    ports:
    - containerPort: 9443
      name: https
      protocol: TCP
--
ROOT CAUSE: The Kubernetes endpoint controller did not consider named ports declared in initContainers with restartPolicy=Always as available ports for Services endpoints. This omission caused Services targeting those named ports to not have corresponding ports listed in their Endpoints resource, preventing traffic from reaching the sidecar container through the Service.
FIX: The name port of the sidecar will also be allowed to be used
FILES: pkg/api/v1/pod/util.go, pkg/api/v1/pod/util_test.go

TITLE: Termination signals not sent to Native Sidecars when multiple Native Sidecars
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In a situation where during the init phase of a `Pod`, a native sidecar never becomes ready (because its `startupProbe` is failing), then the `Pod` is terminated, if there are multiple startup containers, a termination signal is never received by the init container and the Pod is stuck (until `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is hit).

### What did you expect to happen?

All running initContainer to receive the termination signal correctly.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a `Dockerfile` with this bash script as an entrypoint:

```
#!/bin/bash
set -e 
trap 'echo "saw an exit signal"; sleep 5; exit' EXIT

while true; do
  echo "hello"
  sleep 1
done
```

Create a deployment with two init containers (one normal one sidecar).  Add an probe which means the startupProbe never passes

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: karl-test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app2: karl-test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app2: karl-test 
    spec:
      securityContext:
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefaul
ROOT CAUSE: The termination logic failed to send termination signals to restartable init containers when some other restartable init containers had not yet started. This caused pods with multiple native sidecars to block termination signals if one sidecar never became ready during initialization, leaving the pod stuck without proper cleanup.
FIX: Fixed a bug that init containers with `Always` restartPolicy may not terminate gracefully if the pod hasn't initialized yet.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_termination_order.go, test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go

TITLE: sidecar container readniess result to be used in Pod ready state also for pod.spec.restartPolicy = Never or OnFailure
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I created a pod with sidecar container with following manifest:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: simple-webapp
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403

```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger

TITLE: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl g
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that core Kubernetes resource types lacked singular names in their API discovery metadata, unlike CRDs. This omission caused the discovery client cache to prefer a CRD's shortname over the equivalent core resource singular name, leading to inconsistent RESTMapping resolution depending on the order resources were cached and fetched. Without singular names set for core types, the cache could be overwritten unpredictably when a CRD sharing a shortname was queried first.
FIX: Set singular names for core types to pass to discovery

TITLE: KeyEncipherment usage should not be required for non-RSA kubelet client/serving CSRs
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

https://github.com/golang/go/issues/36499 describes why the KeyEncipherment extended key usage does not make sense (and in some cases, is not allowed) for ECDSA keys.

The Kubernetes `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` and `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` signer names require a `key encipherment` usage.

If the kubelet is not using an RSA key (which it does not [by default](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.23.0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L640-L642)), it should not need to specify this key usage.

Since relaxing this to make the `key encipherment` usage optional for those two signerNames may involve an API validation change, this may need rollout over 2 releases. The places we'll need to make sure work properly are:

1. API validation of CSR create and update requests
2. Controller tolerating CSR objects with/without that usage
3. Kubelets requesting CSRs properly without that usage if given a non-RSA key

### What did you expect to happen?

n/a

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

n/a

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes v
ROOT CAUSE: The Kubernetes CSR API required the KeyEncipherment usage for kubelet client and serving certificates regardless of the key type. However, this key usage does not apply to ECDSA keys (which are the default for kubelet), making the requirement incorrect and causing validation failures or unnecessary constraints when non-RSA keys are used.
FIX: Relax API validation for usage key encipherment and kubelet uses requested usages accordingly

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

TITLE: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because a grace period override of 0 was used during eviction to force immediate pod termination, but the pod worker logic interpreted a zero override as no override and used the pod's full configured grace period. This caused evicted and force deleted pods to respect their full termination grace period instead of being terminated immediately. To enforce immediate eviction, a grace period override of 1 second must be used instead of zero.
FIX: Fixes a bug where hard evictions due to resource pressure would let the pod have the full termination grace period, instead of shutting down instantly. This bug also affected force deleted pods. Both cases now get a termination grace period of 1 second.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The TimedWorkerQueue's design to keep keys in its workers map with nil values to prevent duplicated work causes a concurrency bug when a work is cancelled concurrently. Specifically, if CancelWork acquires the lock and deletes the worker key from the map but the wrapped worker function later reacquires the lock and sets the key to nil, the key remains in the map even after cancellation. This leads to future AddWork calls incorrectly skipping work due to the key's presence with a nil value in the map, resulting in taint manager work being unexpectedly skipped and pods stuck in Running state.

claims.text: The TimedWorkerQueue's getWrappedWorkerFunc sets the workers map key to nil after successful work to prevent duplicate work, but CancelWork concurrently deletes the key. If CancelWork deletes the key before the worker function sets it to nil, the key remains in the map with a nil value, causing later AddWork calls to skip the work.

The taint manager triggers pod eviction work via TimedWorkerQueue AddWork and CancelWork calls, so this concurrency bug in TimedWorkerQueue causes taint eviction work to be skipped unexpectedly, leaving pods stuck in Running state instead of transitioning to Terminating.

The ticket's logs show the TimedWorkerQueue adding then cancelling work on the same pod key, followed by skipping adding new work due to the key's lingering presence with a nil value — matching the concurrency bug described in the TimedWorkerQueue code comments and logic.

TITLE: CEL stored messageExpressions of CRDs are not validated with the correct CEL environment
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Noticed a copy & paste issue when reading through the CEL code.

Basically here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/validation/validation.go#L182

This should be 
> expressions.messageExpressions.Insert(v.MessageExpression)
instead of:
> expressions.messageExpressions.Insert(v.Rule)

The impact of this issue should be that messageExpressions are always evaluated with the CEL environment of the compatibility version. But stored (i.e. pre-existing) messageExpressions should be evaluated with a CEL environment with the "max" version instead.

For users of Kubernetes this means that messageExpressions deployed with one minor version of Kubernetes might not work anymore if they rollback e.g. by one minor version.



### What did you expect to happen?

messageExpressions should be treated the same way as rules in that regard.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Deploy Kubernetes 1.30
* Deploy CRD that uses messageExpression that is using Sets (which became available with Kubernetes 1.30 that is using compatibilty version 1.29)
* 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the stored messageExpressions for CRDs were inserted incorrectly using the environment intended for rules rather than being inserted and validated with the correct, up-to-date CEL environment. This caused messageExpressions deployed with a newer Kubernetes version to be validated with an outdated compatibility environment, breaking compatibility on rollback scenarios.
FIX: Validate CRD stored messageExpressions with the correct CEL environment

ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cel-go library updated its cost estimator for CEL expressions, which changed the estimated resource cost of CRD validation rules between Kubernetes versions 1.27 and 1.28. This led to previously acceptable validation rules being rejected due to exceeding the cost budget without changes in the rule itself, causing a backward compatibility break in CRD validation cost enforcement.

TITLE: CEL estimated cost treats enums as strings of unbounded length
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

@robscott pointed out to me that a CEL x-kubernetes-validations rule in a CRD was hitting the estimated cost limit when performing a simple "string has prefix" check on an en enum field.

Putting a `maxLength` limit in the OpenAPI of the enum string field fixed the problem, but having to add a limit like this is counter-intuitive and unnecessary, since the allowed enum values already make the max allowed length obvious.

### What did you expect to happen?

The apiserver automatically computes the max length of an enum as the length of the longest allowed enum value. 

I believe we already refuse evaluate CEL rules on values that fail OpenAPI value validation, since we rely in the value validations to establish all length limits.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I haven't tested it locally, but something like this should work (given enough nested arrays):

```
openAPIV3Schema:
  type: object
  properties:
    spec:
      type: array
      items:
        type: array
        nested:
          type: string
          enum: ["low", "medium", "high"]
          x-kubernetes-validations:
            - rul
ROOT CAUSE: The cost estimation logic for CEL validation expressions treated enum string fields as having unbounded length because it did not account for the inherent length limits defined by the enum values. Without setting the maxLength to the longest enum value, the cost estimator assumed maximum length was unbounded, causing higher-than-necessary costs and limits to be hit unexpectedly.
FIX: CEL cost estimator no longer treats enums as unbounded strings when determining its length. Instead, the length is set to the longest possible enum value.
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/compilation_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/registry/customresource/strategy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/common/schemas.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The root cause of the bug is a logic error in the implementation of the `cidrContainsCIDR` CEL function. The function incorrectly constructs the masked prefix of the contained CIDR by using the prefix length of the container CIDR instead of its own prefix length. This causes incorrect masking which breaks the containment logic when CIDRs have different prefix lengths and addresses.

claims.text: The defect lies in the `cidrContainsCIDR` function implementing the CEL check for CIDR containment, where it compares masked prefixes incorrectly by using `cidr.Prefix.Bits()` for the contained CIDR's prefix length instead of `containsCIDR.Prefix.Bits()`. This leads to incorrect masking of the contained CIDR address and breaks the containment check when masks differ.
The ticket reproduces the issue using nested CEL macros in CRD validation, showing that the rule intended to verify CIDR containment fails because the underlying containment logic is flawed.

TITLE: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

Because of the shortened validity period, we rotate the file-based endcerts frequently. Recently we started noticing that after performing a certificate rotation, usage of `kubectl logs` was failing with

```sh
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)
```

From there, we looked at the kube-apiserver and kubelet logs and found log lines like the following:

```
"Unable to authenticate the request due to an error" err="verifying certificate SN=<REMOVED>, SKID=<REMOVED>, AKID=<REMOVED> failed: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2022-12-17T02:31:09Z is after 2022-12-17T00:16:30Z"
```

So it looks like kube-apiserver didn't reload the new kubelet client certificate. This issue typically goes away if we restart the kube-apiserver container or continue to run `kubectl logs` in a loop.

### What did you expect to happen?

Being able to replace/rotate the kube-apiserver kubelet client certificate/key without causing failure for any 
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-apiserver did not reload or re-establish the TLS connections to the kubelet when the client certificate files used for authentication were rotated. Instead, it reused existing cached TLS connections which retained the old, expired certificates, causing authentication failures on subsequent requests such as 'kubectl logs'.
FIX: The Kubernetes API server now correctly detects and closes existing TLS connections when its client certificate file for kubelet authentication has been rotated.

TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger

### What happened?

We are encountering a severe performance issue in kube-proxy (v1.32) when any Pod with a UDP port is updated (e.g., CoreDNS). In the new kube-proxy implementation, changes to Services or Pods that expose UDP ports trigger a full conntrack cleanup. This cleanup process iterates over the entire conntrack table, leading to extremely high resource consumption—sometimes up to 12 GB of memory and 1.5 CPU cores per kube-proxy instance.

In a simple test, we observed 2,780 instances of the log message "Adding conntrack filter for cleanup", which caused an OOM when kube-proxy was limited to 256 MB of memory. Without that limit, kube-proxy memory usage spiked to 12 GB. On nodes with large conntrack tables, kube-proxy effectively becomes stuck, consuming all available memory each time there is a UDP endpoint change.

This issue appears to be systemic; every change in a Pod with a UDP port triggers all kube-proxy instances to perform the extensive cleanup. Currently, there is no option to disable or throttle this behavior, which disrupts cluster stability and can lead to service degradation or outages. We request that the cleanup logic be revised to target only the relevant conntrack entries or that a mechanism be provided to disable or limit this aggressive cleanup behavior.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130

We experienced an EC2 node failure within our EKS cluster. This affected node was running two CoreDNS pods, which are responsible for DNS resolution in our Kubernetes cluster. Envoy connects to CoreDNS through the UDP protocol. After these CoreDNS pods were terminated, Envoy continued to attempt connections to the terminated IP for DNS resolution.
The kube-proxy failed to update the entry in the conntrack tables, causing some Envoy pods to still connect to the terminated CoreDNS pod IP. Once we restarted the Envoy pods, the entry was refreshed, and the DNS timeout issue was resolved.

Mapping in Conntrack table for src pod ip-10.103.83.53 for UDP protocol.

ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the kube-proxy logic incorrectly removed a check that identified when a UDP endpoint changed from a Serving to a non-Serving state, causing conntrack entries for UDP connections not to be deleted when endpoints were no longer serving. TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:

2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e

1. kube-proxy would redeploy (e.g. due to AKS deploying a new kube-proxy image with CVE fixes)
2. Envoy c-ares DNS client would send repeated DNS queries to the kube-dns service VIP from the same src IP address, creating a UDP conntrack entry to the svc VIP and keeping it alive. For example, with kube-dns svc VIP 192.168.0.10, conntrack showed:

kube-proxy code to delete stale UDP conntrack entries should have de

TITLE: "Connection reset by peer" due to invalid conntrack packets
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When packets with sequence number out-of-window arrived k8s node, conntrack marked them as INVALID. kube-proxy will ignore them, without rewriting DNAT. However, there is no corresponding session link on the host, and the host sends a reset packet, causing the session link to be interrupted

### What did you expect to happen?

connection not reset

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839

### Anything else we need to know?

This problem can be solved by command：
iptables -t filter -I INPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate INVALID -j DROP

Similar issue:https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839
But this issue "drop" is placed on the forward chain, our scenario needs to be placed on the input chain.

### Kubernetes version


$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.0", GitCommit:"c2b5237ccd9c0f1d600d3072634ca66cefdf272f", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-08-04T18:03:20Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.0", GitCommit
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because kube-proxy installed an iptables rule that unconditionally dropped packets with an INVALID conntrack state. In some network scenarios, such as nodes with multihoming, legitimate traffic can be mistakenly marked as INVALID by conntrack. Dropping such packets causes unexpected connection resets because kube-proxy does not rewrite DNAT for them. The fix was to make kube-proxy conditionally install these DROP rules only if the system-wide nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal setting is not set, avoiding disruptions from misclassified INVALID packets.
FIX: Kube-proxy will only install the DROP rules for invalid conntrack states if the nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal is not set.
FILES: pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because kube-proxy's conntrack cleanup logic for UDP port changes triggers a full cleanup over the entire conntrack table by generating many filters indiscriminately for all relevant connection entries rather than limiting to only the affected endpoints. This causes a massive invocation of netlink's ConntrackDeleteFilters with a huge number of filter entries, which leads to excessive memory consumption as failed delete attempts are aggregated in a large array inside the third-party vishvananda/netlink library. The excessive accumulation of filters and the lack of a targeted or throttled cleanup mechanism cause kube-proxy to spike to 12 GB memory and very high CPU usage on each UDP pod update.

claims.text: The cleanup logic in pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go constructs many conntrack filters for UDP ports on all service IP and NodePort endpoints when any UDP pod is updated, causing a full conntrack cleanup and high resource consumption.

The functions filterForNAT and filterForPortNAT log thousands of "Adding conntrack filter for cleanup" messages during UDP pod updates, confirming that many filters are created and processed, which correlates with the high memory spike observed in the ticket.

The large number of filters leads to a very large array allocation inside vishvananda/netlink's ConntrackDeleteFilters function to aggregate failures, causing the heavy memory and CPU usage observed in kube-proxy.

TITLE: Pod status phase misses Pending transition after node reboot
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a kubernetes node is rebooted, all the containers running on the node are terminated and then created & started over again. When the pod has a list of init containers runing, and if the init container takes a little bit time (longer than PLEG period), the pod is supposed to have `status.phase: Pending`, but instead, during the whole operation, `status.phase` is always `Running`.

This new behavior (always has `status.phase: Running`) started when "restartable init container" was [introduced][1]. After node reboots, all the regular init containers are started one by one, so `pendingInitialization` is supposed by larger than 0 (unless the init container is completed pretty fast that PLEG doesn't catch any running init container), and should report `Pending` phase. But the behavior has changed to check further whether there are any other regular containers that have started. In the case of node reboot, all the other regular containers are already terminated, and then considered as "yes, they have started", and then no longer reported as `Pending`.

I think this behavior change is unexpected, as that violates the [definition][2] of "Running":

> // PodR
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the pod phase logic was changed to check if any main containers had started, and if so, it would not report the Pod as 'Pending' even when init containers were still running. After a node restart, main containers might appear as started (due to termination and restart process), causing the pod to be incorrectly categorized as 'Running' instead of 'Pending' while init containers still run.
FIX: Fixed a bug where the pod(with regular init containers)'s phase was not pending when the regular init container had not finished running after a node restart.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, test/e2e/framework/pod/wait.go, test/e2e_node/pod_status_test.go

- Kubernetes control plane reports "Orphan pods" on its audit logs

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes Garbage collector to clean up these PODs after the node is gone

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy the following yaml deployments into a K8s cluster 1.26 and terminate one of the nodes

(duplicated port key "containerPort + protocol")

metadata:
  name: nginx

ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is a regression introduced by enabling PodDisruptionConditions by default. This caused the pod garbage collector to fail deleting pods that had duplicated fields such as repeated environment variable keys or container ports, resulting in orphan pods left on non-existent nodes. The garbage collector used Server-Side Apply (SSA) for patching Pod Disruption Conditions, which failed on pods with duplicated fields, blocking cleanup.

TITLE: `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It appears that the `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` is now blocking the apiserver from becoming ready for 1 minute, if discovery for an aggregated apiservice is not available when the apiserver is started. Note that this only happens if the apiservice is marked available when the apiserver is started; if it is unavailable at startup (Available status: false), or the service has no endpoints, the health check does not block and readyz returns `ok` without delay.

I am seeing this behavior in 1.28.1 and 1.28.2, but not v1.27.6 or v1.27.5

apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays

ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by the AddUpdateAPIService function simultaneously adding and updating the APIService spec during startup, rather than deferring the spec update to be handled asynchronously by the controller. FIX: Fix regression with adding aggregated apiservices panicking and affected health check introduced in release v1.28.0

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

```yaml

spec: 
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  hostNetwork: true
  initContainers:

TITLE: Transient Driver Registration on the CSINode can Result in Missed NodeUnstageVolume RPCs During Pod Migration
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In `unmountDetachDevices` (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L279-L316)) we have the following code that will ultimately dispatch `NodeUnstageVolume` RPCs to the underlying CSI plugin.

Here is a pseudo-code representation of the current logic:

```
function unmountDetachDevices
	for all unmounted volumes in ASoW
		if volume not in DSoW &&
		   not operation pending on volume
			if device is mounted globally or
			   device is mounted uncertain
				Case A:
				unmount device
				(this will kick off the NodeUnstageVolume RPC; we want to be here)
			else
				Case B:
				just remove volume from ASoW
				(general badness since we don't issue a NodeUnstageVolume RPC)
```

In our testbeds, we have observed a number of occurrences where we fall into `Case B` when the CSI Node plugin for a particular driver is being bounced, which leads to the volumemanager failing to dispatch the `NodeUnstageVolume` RPC. If the pod migrates to another node, this will leave behind a Zombie LUN in our testbeds (we're using iSCSI).

A Zombie LUN can and often does resu
ROOT CAUSE: The CSI attacher treats the absence of the CSI driver during a NodeStageVolume call as a final error, transitioning volume devices from uncertain to unmounted state prematurely. This causes unmountDetachDevices logic to skip issuing NodeUnstageVolume RPCs, potentially leaving volumes in a zombie state. The root cause is misclassification of a missing CSI driver error as final rather than transient, leading to incorrect device state transitions and missed cleanup calls.
FIX: Retry NodeStageVolume calls if CSI node driver is not running

TITLE: CSI migration race condition can cause unexpected detach and data loss
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L438-L447) BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error

Error creating spec for volume "elasticsearch", pod "XXX"/"elasticsearch-0": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "dXX"/"elasticsearch-elasticsearch-0": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node gke-stage-XXXXX but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed.
```

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as 
ROOT CAUSE: The attach-detach (AD) controller initiated population of the desired state of the world before the CSI driver was fully up and running on the node. Because of this ordering issue (a race condition), the controller failed to recognize the CSI migrated volume properly and therefore triggered an erroneous detach operation on a volume still in use, leading to data corruption.
FIX: Fix an issue where a CSI migrated volume may be prematurely detached when the CSI driver is not running on the node.
If CSI migration is enabled on the node, even the csi-driver is not up and ready, we will still add this volume to DSW.

TITLE: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-i
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the initial list result in the Reflector retains references to a large slice of objects, and if any object pointer from that slice is still in use, the Go runtime keeps the entire backing array in memory. This happens because the ObjectList contains a slice of objects (not pointers), and the Reflector takes pointers to these objects, preventing garbage collection of the initial slice. Thus, memory is not freed even when most objects are deleted or changed, leading to high memory consumption.
FIX: client-go: Improved memory use of reflector caches when watching large numbers of objects which do not change frequently

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. This leads to users receiving misleading or incorrect URLs without an obvious indication that an earlier error occurred during request construction.

TITLE: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and p
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cacher's readiness blocking mechanism was implemented using a sync.Cond variable that did not support context cancellation or timeouts. As a result, watch requests waiting for the cacher to become ready could be blocked indefinitely if the cacher was never marked ready, leading to infinite wait and resource exhaustion in concurrency queues.
FIX: cacher allow context cancellation if not ready

Please note that there are other members (not related to retry logic) of `Request` that are not thread safe depending on how different methods of a `Request` object is used from multiple go routines.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217/files#r837633535

Also, the comments on some of these methods and sections for retry logic can be improved:
- For instance, we may want to rename `IsErrorRetryable` to `IsHttpErrRetryable` and `checkWait` to `isServerIndicatedRetry`. 
That would have helped bring this back into mental cache faster and possibly help some future refactorer.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because client timeout errors during watch event decoding are masked as io.ErrShortBuffer by the framer's Read method, causing the StreamWatcher to interpret them as internal server errors. This leads the reflector to treat these errors as unrecoverable internal errors and trigger expensive relist operations instead of retrying watch resumption. The masking of the original timeout error disables the retry logic condition, causing unnecessary relists on transient client-side timeouts.

claims.text: Reflector.go uses ShouldRetry to distinguish recoverable watch errors that merit a watch retry versus those requiring a relist. The bug occurs because ShouldRetry returns false on InternalErrors generated from masked client timeout errors, leading to relist every time.
The lengthDelimitedFrameReader's Read method masks client timeout errors by replacing the actual timeout error with io.ErrShortBuffer, thus hiding the real error from higher layers.

The streaming decoder detects io.ErrShortBuffer and returns a custom error message, further masking the original timeout error causing the watcher to see a misleading error indicative of a short buffer rather than a timeout.

StreamWatcher.receive interprets errors that are not recognized as timeouts or EOFs as internal server errors, so the masked error results in an InternalError event, triggering the reflector to relist instead of retrying watch continuation.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the allocator code handling the 'All' allocationMode does not properly check if any devices are actually available on the node before allowing allocation. When a node has zero devices of the requested class, the requestData.allDevices slice is empty and requestData.numDevices is zero, but the allocator does not fail allocation accordingly and allows the pod to be scheduled. This leads to pods being scheduled on nodes that have no devices matching the claim, violating the intended semantics that 'All' means at least one device must be present.

claims.text: The allocator code from allocator.go builds the list of all devices for the allocationMode 'All' but when there are zero devices on the node, it sets requestData.numDevices to 0 without any special guard or error, allowing subsequent allocation to incorrectly succeed.

The recursive allocation logic in allocateOne does not specially handle the case where numDevices is zero in 'All' mode and proceeds with allocation, leading to pods scheduled on nodes with zero devices.

The report in the ticket describes how a pod requesting 'All' GPUs scheduled onto a node with no DRA driver running and no resource slices present, indicating that the current implementation does not prevent scheduling in the empty device case.
