TITLE: Flag to Disable the 6-minute Force Detach Window
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Certain online upgrade workflows might need to restart kubernetes as a part of their upgrade procedure. This can lead to the following sequence:
* As a part of draining a kubernetes node, a pod might get deleted.
* The unmount of a pod could take more than 6 minutes.
* If the node is deemed unhealthy when the 6 minute timer fires for the pod being deleted (for example, because kubelet is still restarting), then the underlying PV will be force detached (via a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPC)

These workflows would likely benefit from disabling this feature in lieu of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature that hit GA in kubernetes 1.28 (see [here](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/) for more details).

When these issues are encountered in our testbeds, we are left with Zombie iSCSI LUNs. If pods end up migrating to a node with such a Zombie LUN present, those pods might end up attaching themselves to the Zombie LUN leading to data corruption.

This data corruption has caused a number of our cluster-management applications to lose all access to their data, requiring them to be deployed from scratch (occasi
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because there is a built-in 6-minute timeout after which volumes are force detached if the node is unhealthy, regardless of whether the pod has successfully unmounted the volume. This force detachment can cause persistent volumes to become stuck in a 'Zombie' state, leading to data corruption when pods attach to these stale volumes. The root cause is the rigid 6-minute force detach window that triggers detach operations without accounting for longer unmount durations and node restart circumstances.
FIX: This change adds the following CLI option for `kube-controller-manager`:
* `disable-force-detach` (defaults to `false`): Prevent force detaching volumes based on maximum unmount time and node status. If enabled, the non-graceful node shutdown feature must be used to recover from node failure (see https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/). If enabled and a pod must be forcibly terminated at the risk of corruption, then the appropriate VolumeAttachment object (see here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/volume-attachment-v1/) must be deleted.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/options/attachdetachcontroller.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller_test.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/config/types.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/config/v1alpha1/zz_generated.conversion.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go, pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler_test.go, pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go, staging/src/k8s.io/kube-controller-manager/config/v1alpha1/types.go

diagnosis.root_cause: Starting from Kubernetes 1.30, the kubectl exec command uses a WebSocket-based remote command executor by default instead of SPDY. This WebSocketExecutor implementation, triggered by the new default behavior or the feature-gate/environment variable RemoteCommandWebsockets, causes idle exec sessions to be disconnected after about 5 minutes due to handling or timeout issues in the websocket streaming code. This behavior did not occur in earlier versions which used SPDY streaming by default, and switching back to SPDY by setting KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS=false avoids the disconnection issue.

claims.text: The kubectl exec implementation in exec.go switched from SPDY streaming by default to WebSocket streaming starting in version 1.30, as seen by the use of WebSocketExecutor and WebSocket protocol versions in the code.

Users report the session disconnects in about 5 minutes starting with 1.30 but not before, and disabling WebSocket mode by setting KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS=false reverts to the older SPDY method which fixes the disconnect issue.

The code change causing the use of WebSocket streaming by default introduced unexpected disconnects for idle sessions possibly due to WebSocket handling or timeout defects, hence the bug is a logic error in the kubectl exec code implementing WebSocket streams.

triage.summary: The DeletionTimestamp on a Pod after a delete request does not consistently include the termination grace period that was respected; the final DeletionTimestamp set by the APIServer reflects immediate deletion time rather than accounting for the grace period, resulting in unexpected behavior especially when kubelet delays deletion.

evidence.text:
DeletionTimestamp set after grace period is respected does not include grace period time
Dear Kubernetes-Team:

I ran an experiment with an application that does not exit after Kubelet sends an inital SIGTERM signal.
The specified grace-period is respected and the pod is deleted after the grace period finishes.

The deletionTimestamp on the inital delete event seems to include the grace-period, but the deletionTimestamp that is finally updated by the APIServer does not account for the grace-period that was respected. This DeletionTimestamp is also seen when the DeleteFunc is triggered on separate podInformers we have running on our clusters.

I have attached some test results detailing this below; This behavior seems like a bug. The final DeletionTimestamp that is updated by the APIServer should indeed include any grace-period that was respected. (Ideally it should be when the application exits, and not just at the time the user puts in the delete request)


My experiment is as follows:

1) Create a busybox pod with a termination grace period (for example 5 mins)
2) Call delete pod
3) APIServer gets a delete event initiated by the user (k8s-admin) with a deletion timestamp by adding the 5 mins grace period
4) After the grace period ends api server gets another delete event from kubelet (system:node:fargate-ip-19)
5) This delete event from kubelet has grace period of 0 and the DeletionTimestamp set to when user deleted the pod (instead of that time + the respected grace period)

The podspec `busybox.yaml` that is applied: 
```
apiVersion: v1
k

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because the Kubernetes apiserver's delete request processing logic recalculates and sets the object's DeletionTimestamp in a way that can move it backward to the original user deletion time when kubelet submits a delete with a zero grace period. This logic subtracts the original grace period and adds the new grace period without ensuring the new timestamp does not precede the current time or the already respected grace period, causing the final DeletionTimestamp to ignore the actual grace period respected by kubelet and thus appear as if it did not include it.

claims.text: The apiserver delete logic adjusts DeletionTimestamp by subtracting the original grace period and adding the new grace period when kubelet sends a delete with grace period 0, resetting DeletionTimestamp back to the user delete time rather than the actual later deletion time.

The ticket's experiment shows that initial DeletionTimestamp includes the grace period, but the final DeletionTimestamp after kubelet deletion reverts to the original deletion time, losing the grace period.

Discussion references the relevant code in rest/delete.go that causes DeletionTimestamp to move backwards on kubelet requests, which kubelet sends with grace period 0 and deletion timestamp matching the original user deletion time.

Kubernetes API guarantees that DeletionTimestamp can never be set in the future or extended, only moved backwards, which the current code enforces but leads to this problem where the timestamp ignores the actually respected grace period.

TITLE: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

spec:

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go, pkg/kubelet/kubelet_test.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go, pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go, pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/fake_pod_deletion_safety.go, pkg/kubelet/status/testing/mock_pod_status_provider.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because during a pod update, the ResourceQuota controller calculates the delta resource usage by subtracting the usage of the old object from the new object without accounting for a possible change in quota scopes. If a pod transitions from one quota scope to another (e.g., from NotTerminating to Terminating), this calculation erroneously results in zero delta usage, causing the quota controller to skip updating usage counts, and thus the quota usage becomes stale and incorrect.

claims.text: During pod update, the delta usage is computed as the difference between the new pod's usage and the old pod's usage without factoring in that the pod's quota scope may have changed, leading to zero delta and no quota update.

The ticket clearly describes that when a pod transitions from one quota scope to another, the quota usage is not updated because the delta calculation does not consider scope changes, leading to stale quota usage.

TITLE: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as po
ROOT CAUSE: The code for constructing REST requests accumulates errors internally but the URL() method ignores any existing errors and returns a URL regardless. FIX: client-go: add an Error() function on Request

This does not seem to cause any user facing problem because `EphemeralContainerStatuses` is sorted before passed to the status manager and timestamps are normalized at marshaling to create a patch:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2336

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cade1dddd81eba338df85de7b5d17324a87243b5/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L873

If a pod has an init container with restartPolicy "Always" (sidecar), it may lose the pending phase after the node reboot and start the regular containers before initializing the init containers.



This is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126650, but separated as it only affects the pod with restartable init containers.

### What did you expect to happen?

After the node reboot, the remaining pod should start from the pending phase and run the init containers one by one to initialize.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create and initialize the pod with an init container with "Always" container restart policy.
2. Restart the node.

### Anything else we need to know?

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version

TITLE: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What 
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet did not transition deleted pods that are still in the Running or Pending phase to a terminal phase (Succeeded or Failed) even when their containers had terminated and would not be restarted due to their RestartPolicy. This caused deleted pods to remain stuck in Running or Pending state indefinitely.
FIX: Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.

TITLE: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Scheduler should use max(Spec.Resources.Requests, Status.Resources.Requests) instead of Status.AllocatedResources
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Current implementation of in-place pod resize looks at max(Spec.Resources, Status.Resources) which works well when resources are being increased, and works well when resources are being decreased assuming that the decrease request is based on observed lower usage, and the new lowered resources does not exceed current usage.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d86b74b0176c6fa22ba2559ace961fa25c6e98cf/pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go#L64-L73

However, a bad actor can game the system by requesting resize to resources lower than current usage, and kubelet grants it not knowing that runtime cannot enforce it, and scheduler may schedule pods to an oversubscribed node. A simple way to avoid this is to use Status.Resources.Requests instead of Status.AllocatedResources.

This also means that containerd and other runtimes need to be at a version that supports the feature so that users get the correct signals (avoid 'forever InProgress')


### What did you expect to happen?

When desired resources are lowered and kubelet admits it and sets status to InProgress, scheduler should schedule new pods against resources that are actually available. Bad actors sho
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler made scheduling decisions based on the max of requested and status resources without considering that the kubelet might have admitted a decrease below current actual usage. This allowed pods to be resized to resource amounts lower than what the runtime could enforce, causing potential oversubscription and incorrect scheduling.
FIX: ContainerStatus.AllocatedResources is now guarded by a separate feature gate, InPlacePodVerticalSaclingAllocatedStatus

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…

When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.

If p1 scheduling attempt happens before p2's nominated_node_name is cleared, the scheduler mistakenly considers insufficient memory and delays scheduling p1 by several minutes. This stems from unsynchronized handling of pod nomination clearing and pod re-adding causing stale scheduling state and blocked scheduling retries.

TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.
FIX: Add implementation for PodRecreationPolicy to wait for creation of pods once the existing ones are fully terminated.

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml

kind: Job
metadata:
  name: inde
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the Job was marked as Failed or Completed as soon as failure or success conditions were met, without waiting for all Pods to reach a terminal state. This caused running Pods to still be counted as ready, leading to inaccurate accounting in higher-level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
FIX: Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/endpointslicecache.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/service.go, pkg/proxy/service_test.go

TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go, pkg/proxy/types.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the HNS load balancer update in the Windows kube-proxy relies on caching load balancer information keyed by a hash of endpoints, but the hash or the cache is not correctly updated on endpoint changes. claims.text: The updateLoadBalancer function recreates the load balancer with the new endpoints and caches the load balancer info keyed by a hash of endpoints, so if the hash or cache equality check is flawed, endpoint updates could be stale.
The ticket describes the symptom as endpoints not being updated in HNS after ModifyLoadBalancer API calls by Windows kube-proxy, consistent with stale caching behavior in the proxier code.

triage.summary: Kubelet's pod status update merges its internal status with API status but does not sync PodResizeStatus properly, causing a race condition where the Kubelet may overwrite the 'Proposed' resize status with stale data, leading to inconsistency.

evidence.text:
[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Race condition setting pod resize status
The kubelet updates the pod status by first generating the pod status based on its internal representation, and then [merging](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1049) that with the latest status from the API, based on whether the Kubelet should be the source of truth for those fields.

Currently, the PodResizeStatus is not synced with the API server status, which means that whatever the Kubelet thinks the resize status should be will overwrite whatever PodResizeStatus is currently stored in the API server. This can lead to a race condition where the Kubelet has not yet seen a resize update, and clobbers the `Proposed` resize status.

I'm not sure exactly what the right behavior is here, but it probably needs to be an intelligent state transition, or may require comparing resource versions.

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

Then restart kubelet for the first ti
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the kubelet assigned an empty or zero value to resource requests (like memory) that were not defined in the container spec when storing resource allocations in the checkpoint file. diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the kubelet's merge logic for pod status updates does not specifically handle PodResizeStatus fields, leading to the kubelet overwriting the API server's current resize status with its own internal state. Since the PodResizeStatus is not synchronized or merged intelligently, race conditions arise where the kubelet may clobber 'Proposed' resize statuses that it has not yet observed, due to asynchronous updates and lack of version or state checks.

claims.text: The ticket explains that the kubelet updates pod status by merging its internal status with the latest API server status, but PodResizeStatus is not synced, causing kubelet's internal status to overwrite the API server's status, leading to race conditions where Proposed resize statuses are lost.

The mergePodStatus function (status_manager.go L1049-1120) merges old and new pod status without any specific synchronization or merge logic for PodResizeStatus, so kubelet's status overwrites the API server's without checking for race conditions or state transitions, consistent with the reported race.

The updateStatusInternal function (status_manager.go L603-721) updates the cached pod status and queues API server update by merging statuses but does not handle PodResizeStatus explicitly, allowing kubelet's internal resize status to overwrite the API server's current resize status without syncing or state validation, facilitating race conditions noted in the ticket.

TITLE: NodeExpandVolume gets called, even if CSI plugin returned NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In case of online volume expansion of raw block volumes, some of the CSI plugins may not need file system resize or any related handling and thus NodeExpandVolume API call can be skipped for the same. In order to do this, plugin must set NodeExpansionRequired to false, in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse.
However, it is observed that kubelet does call NodeExpandVolume API, after successful resize done by CSI plugin in ControllerExpandVolume API call with NodeExpansionRequired=false in response.
Even though CSI plugin can skip handling in NodeExpandVolume API as per its requirement, is it expected to get this API call from kubelet when NodeExpansionRequired set to false by plugin in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse?

### What did you expect to happen?

During CSI volume online expansion, if CSI plugin returns NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse, to indicate no FS resize handling needed, then kubelet should not call NodeExpandVolume API for such volume(s).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The issue is seen with vSphere CSI driver, while expanding vSphere raw-block volume (volumeMode: Block), 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the kubelet does not respect the NodeExpansionRequired=false flag returned by CSI plugins in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse and still calls the NodeExpandVolume API unnecessarily. This incorrect handling causes extra API calls when the plugin has indicated no node-side expansion is required.
FIX: Promoted `RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure` feature gate to beta.

TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic

TITLE: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-proxy component lacked a properly configured --nodeport-addresses setting in a dual-stack environment, causing it to listen on all IP interfaces (0.0.0.0 and ::) by default. This results in healthCheckNodePort binding to all zeros (wildcard address) instead of a node's specific IP, because the code defaults to listening on all addresses if no specific nodeport address ranges are configured.
FIX: The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The kubelet tracks pod dynamic resource preparation state based on an assumption that NodePrepareResources has been successfully called if attempted, thus blocking pod deletion while trying to call NodeUnprepareResources regardless of actual preparation success. This logic fails when NodePrepareResources is never successfully issued, causing the kubelet to hang on pod deletion, as it awaits an unprepare step for a resource that was never allocated.

claims.text: The kubelet tries to unprepare dynamic resources on pod deletion assuming NodePrepareResources was issued, but the pod state does not record if preparation was actually done, leading to deletion hang if preparation failed or was never done.

No functions named NodePrepareResources or NodeUnprepareResources were found in the scheduler dynamicresources plugin, indicating the relevant logic is likely in the kubelet's DRA manager, specifically pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go.

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

TITLE: Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:
```
E1127 19:48:13.221979   66549 schedule_one.go:130] "Error selecting node for pod" err="applying score defaultWeights on Score plugins: plugin \"PodTopologySpread\" returns an invalid score 300, it should in the range of [0, 100] after normalizing" pod="default/test-multi-point-xxxxxxxx"
```

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tai
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the scheduler framework's logic to build plugin lists when merging MultiPoint plugins and regular plugins had a flaw in a loop that led to the same scoring plugin being included multiple times. This caused plugins like PodTopologySpread to execute NormalizeScore multiple times on the same node, producing invalid scores outside the expected [0, 100] range.
FIX: Fixed a regression since 1.24 in the scheduling framework when overriding MultiPoint plugins (e.g. default plugins).
The incorrect loop logic might lead to a plugin being loaded multiple times, consequently preventing any Pod from being scheduled, which is unexpected.
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework_test.go

The error message is hardcoded and does not include dynamic conflict details, causing misleading information that states multiple nodes have conflicts when only specific pods prevent scheduling. This inaccurate counting and generic messaging lead to confusion about the true scheduling constraint.

claims.text: The function calPreFilterState counts conflicting PVC usage by incrementing an integer for each conflicting PVC without accurately representing the number or identity of nodes or pods using the PVC, leading to misleading conflict counts driving the error message.

The satisfyReadWriteOncePod function returns a generic unschedulable status with a hardcoded error reason when conflicts exist, without appending actual conflict details such as counts or pod/node identifiers, causing confusion.

The Filter method calls satisfyReadWriteOncePod and returns its generic error message, which does not clarify the nature or scope of the conflict, resulting in misleading scheduler events that report multiple nodes but ignore actual pod binding details.

The ticket explicitly describes error messages mentioning 5 nodes having conflicting pods using the same PVC with ReadWriteOncePod mode, while in reality only one pod blocks scheduling, reflecting the underlying inaccurate conflict counting and generic messaging in the plugin code.

TITLE: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

```
Jul 25 1
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is a concurrency race in kubelet's device manager when allocating GPU devices to pods. The mutex guarding the allocated devices map is unlocked while calling out to device plugins, allowing concurrent updates and leading to inconsistent or nil map values. This causes the allocation function to panic due to nil map assignments when multiple GPU-using pods are created or deleted concurrently.
FIX: Fix kubelet panic when allocate resource for pod.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager_test.go

triage.summary: The `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)` setting does not disable pod backoff as expected; pods still experience up to ~0.999 seconds of backoff due to a condition comparing backoffTime with truncated current time in backoff queue logic.

evidence.text:
`WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` isn't accurately respected after SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ feature
### What happened?

Let's say you specify `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, you would expect the backoff is disabled completely.
However, actually the pods could experience a backoff penalty for ~0.999 seconds.

It's caused by:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a3097010faac734fb4956dbc91ae9034d0a9f840/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/backoff_queue.go#L211-L212

So, it regards the pod is backing off if `backoffTime == Truncate(now)`.
And, if you specify `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, backoffTime would always be `pInfo.Timestamp`, which is when the pod came back to the queue. Meaning, pods is regarded as backing off until ~1 second has passed after the pod came back to the queue because of `Truncate(now)`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` should be respected as an actual upper limit.
I guess if `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` is set to non-zero value, users notice this problem less likely. 
But, if it's set to 0, users could notice/be confused because they expect no backoff at all, but logs/metrics would show some pods have experienced backoff.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Set `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration(0)`, put a pod in the queue via `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` (simulating the pod is unschedulable and coming back to the queue), immediately trigger some events that trigger the pod's requeueing, and see logs. 
You should see the pod is going through backoffQ.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No

TITLE: scheduler: move all preCheck to QueueingHint
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In our custom plugin, we want to move pods that is unscheduled by the plugin to activeQ/backoffQ when a new Pod is created.
So, we define `EventsToRegister` like this:

```go
func (p *Plugin) EventsToRegister() []framework.ClusterEvent {
	return []framework.ClusterEvent{{
		Resource:   framework.Node,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}, {
		Resource:   framework.Pod,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}}
}
```

But, even when a new Pod is created, the Pod that was unscheduled by our custom plugin isn't moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### What did you expect to happen?

when a new Pod is created, the Pod unscheduled by our custom plugin is moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a custom plugin that has pod events in EventsToRegister.
2. create a new Pod that the custom plugin will reject.
3. create another new Pod that makes the Pod created in (1) schedulable.
4. you can see the Pod created in (1) isn't scheduled immediately (it should've been scheduled immediately after (3) because (3) should move the Pod created in (1) to activeQ/backoffQ.)

### Anything else we need to know
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduling queue's preCheck mechanism assumes a scheduler configuration with only built-in plugins and does not handle external/custom plugins properly, causing pods rejected by these custom plugins to not be moved to the active or backoff queue when new Pods are created. This incompatibility leads to pods staying unscheduled because QHint replaces preCheck's functionality but isn't designed for extensibility with custom plugins.
FIX: feat: disable preCheck when QHint is enabled
FILES: pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue.go, pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go, pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers_test.go

TITLE: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.


### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

_No response_

ROOT CAUSE: The backoff delay calculation for recreating pods in a Job controller excluded pods whose failures matched an 'Ignore' rule in the Job's failure policy. TITLE: Assigned Pod add/update events don't requeue Pods without PodAffinity
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?



- AssignedPodAdded(): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b529e6ff1c7edb3bb1eaca185b9662d8e42ac2d0/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1044
- AssignedPodUpdated(): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b529e6ff1c7edb3bb1eaca185b9662d8e42ac2d0/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1069


When assigned Pods are created/updated, cluster events (Pod/Add or Pod/Update) should be delivered for all plugins that subscribe those events. But, actually `getUnschedulablePodsWithMatchingAffinityTerm` pre-filters Pods to receive those events based on Pods' affinity and `pod.Status.Resize`. - meaning only PodAffinity/NodeResourceFit receive them actually.

The problem here is similar to #110175 - in in-tree plugins, PodAffinity, PodTopologySpread and NodeResourceFit subscribe Pod add and/or update events. And, Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread will never be requeued to activeQ by Pod-related events. The same happens for custom plugins registering pod add and/or update events.


### What did you expect to happen?

All Pods will get chances to get back to activeQ by Pod-related events.

### How can we reproduce it (a
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the mechanism that requeued Pods on pod add/update events filtered Pods only based on PodAffinity and resizing status, ignoring Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread. This selective event delivery prevented Pods rejected by PodTopologySpread and other plugins with similar event subscriptions from being requeued after pod-related events, causing them to get stuck unrescheduled.
FIX: Fix a bug that when PodTopologySpread rejects Pods, they may be stuck in Pending state for 5 min in a worst case scenario.
The same problem could happen with custom plugins which have Pod/Add or Pod/Update in EventsToRegister,
which is also solved with this PR, but only when the feature flag SchedulerQueueingHints is enabled.

diagnosis.root_cause: The backoffQueue's backoff expiration time is always truncated to a 1-second window, causing the condition `backoffTime == Truncate(now)` to consider pods as backing off for up to ~0.999 seconds even when `WithPodMaxBackoffDuration` is set to zero (disabling backoff). This occurs because the pod's backoff expiration time is stored as the pod's timestamp plus backoff duration, truncated to the window, and when the max backoff is zero, this expiration equals the truncated current time, triggering the backoff condition incorrectly.

claims.text: The bug arises due to the equality comparison between the pod's backoff expiration time and the current time truncated to a window, causing pods to be mistakenly considered as backing off for nearly 1 second after requeue when backoff duration is zero.

The backoff expiration time is computed as the pod timestamp plus backoff duration, truncated to the scheduler's backoff ordering window, and for zero max backoff duration, this calculation results in expiration time equaling truncated current time which triggers backing off incorrectly.

TITLE: Code Generation Produces Ambiguous Fields and Duplicate Methods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The changes introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121439 require that all types used with the generated clients implement both `runtime.Object` and `meta.Object`. In order to comply with this, we started embedding `metav1.ObjectMeta` in our API types that were missing it. However, we noticed that, for some of our types, the generator generates code with ambiguous fields and duplicate methods.

For example, consider the following case where both `metav1.ObjectMeta` and `MyEmbeddedType`, which are embedded in `MyType`, contain a `Namespace` field:

```


type MyType struct {
	metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
	metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

	MyEmbeddedType `json:"myEmbeddedType"`
}

type MyEmbeddedType struct {
	Namespace string `json:"namespace"`
}
```

This will generate code like:

```
func (b *MyTypeApplyConfiguration) WithNamespace(value string) *MyTypeApplyConfiguration {
	b.ensureObjectMetaApplyConfigurationExists()
	b.Namespace = &value
	return b
}
```

Here, `b.Namespace` is invalid because that field is present in both embedded types.



### What did you expect to happen?

Generat
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the code generator (applyconfiguration-gen) does not handle the presence of multiple embedded structs that contain fields with the same name. This leads the generator to produce methods and field accesses that are ambiguous or duplicated because it does not qualify or differentiate these fields based on their embedding types. The defect is that applyconfiguration-gen assumes unique member names at the top level without considering embedded struct conflicts.
FIX: applyconfiguration-gen no longer generates duplicate methods and ambiguous member accesses when types end up with multiple members of the same name (through embedded structs).
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/examples/client-go/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/cr/v1/example.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/apiextensions/v1/customresourcedefinition.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/client/applyconfiguration/apiextensions/v1beta1/customresourcedefinition.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/mutatingwebhookconfiguration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/namedrulewithoperations.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/rulewithoperations.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingadmissionpolicy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingadmissionpolicybinding.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/validatingwebhookconfiguration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1alpha1/namedrulewithoperations.go

TITLE: Generated OpenAPI Defaults often do not fit type
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I am working on [kubectl-validate](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubectl-validate/) and see that the populated defaults  for many fields don't themselves pass validation in the OpenAPI published by k8s used by the tool. This means when users leave the fields unspecified the document fails validation. 

This is only a problem for OpenAPI based tools since validation is performed with human written code today, but [KEP-3937](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3937) adds another motivation to ensure the published definitions are accurate for native types:

metav1 has quite a few examples

array with a map default:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1193ab62e2e1acb53edf5348df6fe018cbe49e82/pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go#L49758


another array with map default:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1193ab62e2e1acb53edf5348df6fe018cbe49e82/pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go#L50147

a string with a map default:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1193ab62e2e1acb53edf5348df6fe018cbe49e82/pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go#L49118

### What did you expect to happen?


ROOT CAUSE: The root cause was that the OpenAPI specification generation included invalid default values such as empty maps for fields that have custom marshalling logic, which resulted in defaults that did not conform to their schema types and thus fail validation. diagnosis.root_cause: The kubelet's DRA ManagerImpl unprepareResources function can skip unpreparing resource claims if the claim info is not found in the cache or still referenced by other pods, particularly when pods have zero terminationGracePeriod causing immediate removal. This leads to races where the claim info cache loses track of dynamically allocated claims, resulting in failed container setups due to missing claim info while trying to start the pod. The issue manifests because UnprepareResources does not block pod resource removal until unprepare completes, and the claim cache is not properly synchronized with pod lifecycle events under stress concurrency conditions.

claims.text: The ticket describes a stress test where rapidly starting and stopping pods with the same ResourceClaim causes kubelet to permanently fail container setup with error 'unable to get claim info for claim external-claim in namespace default'. This indicates a race in claim cache handling.

The UnprepareResources function unprepares resource claims for a pod but does not explicitly block pod resource removal until unprepare finishes, potentially causing a race if unprepare is skipped or delayed.

The unprepareResources method skips unpreparing if claimInfo is missing or if other pods still reference the claim, which can cause losing track of claims especially when pods are removed immediately (zero terminationGracePeriod), thus leading to cache inconsistencies.

The stack trace from the ticket shows that GetResources fails to find claim info for the claim during container start, due to missing or stale claim info in the cache caused by races during pod removal and claim unprepare.

TITLE: Sometime Liveness/Readiness Probes fail because of net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
SYMPTOM: **What happened**:
In my cluster sometimes readiness the probes are failing. But the application works fine.
```
Apr 06 18:15:14 kubenode** kubelet[34236]: I0406 18:15:14.056915   34236 prober.go:111] Readiness probe for "default-nginx-daemonset-4g6b5_default(a3734646-77fd-11ea-ad94-509a4c9f2810):nginx" failed (failure): Get http://172.18.123.127:80/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```

**What you expected to happen**:
Successful Readiness Probe.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
We have few clusters with different workloads.
Only in cluster with big number of short living pods we have this issue.
But not on all nodes.
We can't reproduce this error on other our clusters (that have same configuration but different workload).
How i found the issue?
I deployed a daemonset:
```
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: default-nginx-daemonset
  namespace: default
  labels:
    k8s-app: default-nginx
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: default-nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: default-nginx

ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that kubelet readiness and liveness probes open many short-lived network connections that enter the TIME-WAIT state, which by default lasts 60 seconds. This causes exhaustion of network resources like ephemeral ports and conntrack entries on nodes with many pods and high probe rates, leading to probe failures.
FIX: kubelet TCP and HTTP probes are more effective using networking resources: conntrack entries, sockets, ... 
This is achieved by reducing the TIME-WAIT state of the connection to 1 second, instead of the defaults 60 seconds. This allows kubelet to free the socket, and free conntrack entry and ephemeral port associated.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/prober/scale_test.go, pkg/probe/dialer_others.go, pkg/probe/dialer_windows.go, pkg/probe/http/http.go, pkg/probe/tcp/tcp.go

TITLE: kube-apiserver using unregistered and unusual label
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The code at
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86f3fa94f1b75da275a8040e4155840a7b473dc1/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L126 specifies a ~annotation~ label that API servers set on Leases (each API server registers its own lease).

https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/#api-server-identity is likely to document this once v1.26 is released; the alpha for API server identity didn't get documented.

Here's the problems:
- as a project, we use `kubernetes.io` as the domain for labels and annotations - see https://k8s.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/
  - there are a couple of exceptions in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/audit-annotations/, FWIW
- if we document and register this `k8s.io/component` label, people may well confuse it with https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component and use the wrong thing

### What did you expect to happen?

I guess ideally we'd have proposed and then been able to review docs for this when it went alpha, and in that alternative history the discrepancy would have been much more obvious, and it could have been fixed 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the API server was using a non-standard, unregistered label `k8s.io/component` for identifying leases, which conflicted with Kubernetes label conventions and could be easily confused with an existing well-known label `app.kubernetes.io/component`. This violated Kubernetes labeling best practices and conventions causing potential confusion and improper usage.
FIX: Renamed API server identity Lease labels to use the key `apiserver.kubernetes.io/identity`

TITLE: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Tr
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the apiserver's request-timeout enforcement does not cover the duration spent decoding data fetched from etcd. When a large list request is served, the total time including multiple pages fetched and JSON decoding can exceed the timeout without being interrupted, resulting in request latency longer than configured. This is because the timeout mechanism only covers the etcd fetch phase but not the decoding phase.
FIX: Add apiserver.latency.k8s.io/decode-response-object annotation to the audit log to record the decoding time

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because when a list request includes a large resourceVersion parameter together with a limit parameter, the Kubernetes API server bypasses the internal watch cache and queries etcd directly. Etcd returns a specific error "mvcc: required revision is a future revision" for resourceVersions that are not yet available, but the API server does not properly translate this into a 504 (Timeout) status. Instead, the raw etcd error is returned with a 500 status, violating expected API semantics.

claims.text: The 500 error with the message "etcdserver: mvcc: required revision is a future revision" is triggered when both a large resourceVersion and a limit parameter are passed in the request, as described in the bug report's reproduction steps and observed behavior.

When the limit parameter is omitted but the resourceVersion remains large, the request correctly returns a 504 timeout error with the expected message "Too large resource version", indicating that the watch cache handles this case properly and respects resourceVersion semantics.

The presence of the limit parameter causes the API server to bypass the watch cache and query etcd directly, leading to the etcd-specific error not being converted correctly by the API server into a 504 timeout error, which demonstrates improper error handling in the path that queries storage (etcd) directly.

This is classified as an error_handling defect because the API server mishandles etcd errors by directly propagating internal etcd errors as HTTP 500 responses instead of mapping them to appropriate API status codes and messages as per API contract.

TITLE: Fixes in cel-go breaks backward compatible of CRD validation rules between 1.27 and 1.28 release
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We were using cel-go v0.12.7 in Kubernetes 1.27 release and cel-go v0.16.0 in Kubernetes 1.28 release. There are many changes from cel-go side between those two releases and some may break backward compatible of CRD validation rules.

An example would be the estimated cost for CRD validation rules(Thanks to @inteon who brought this to our attention with the following example).
In the example CRD validation rules below:
```
---
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: resources.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Resource
    listKind: ResourceList
    plural: resources
    singular: resource
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1alpha1
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        properties:
          apiVersion:
            type: string
          kind:
            type: string
          metadata:
            type: object
          spec:
            items:
              properties:
                a:
                  type: string
                b:
                  type: string
                c:
                  type: string
                d:
     
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the cel-go library updated its cost estimator for CEL expressions, which changed the estimated resource cost of CRD validation rules between Kubernetes versions 1.27 and 1.28. This led to previously acceptable validation rules being rejected due to exceeding the cost budget without changes in the rule itself, causing a backward compatibility break in CRD validation cost enforcement.
FIX: When updating a CRD, per-expression cost limit check is skipped for x-kubernetes-validations rules of versions that are not mutated.
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/validation/validation.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/validation/validation_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the cost estimator for the extended CEL library, which includes functions like the authorizer requestResource check, was not registered in the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy admission path. Consequently, the CEL runtime cost for these extended library functions was not accurately calculated, leading to underestimation of expression costs and making cost limits ineffective for expressions invoking authorization checks.

claims.text: The ticket states that the cost estimator for the extended library was not registered which caused inaccurate cost calculation for expressions including extended library functions like authorizer.requestResource.check.

In the compilation.go file, the compileRule function shows explicit wiring of cel.CostTracking with a cost estimator for CRD validation rules but this wiring was missing for ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, causing cost tracking to default to minimal costs.

The CostEstimator implementation in library/cost.go assigns a nontrivial fixed cost for expensive functions like 'check', meaning that without registering the CostEstimator, those expensive functions have cost underestimated as 1.

TITLE: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Tr
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the apiserver's request-timeout enforcement does not cover the duration spent decoding data fetched from etcd. When a large list request is served, the total time including multiple pages fetched and JSON decoding can exceed the timeout without being interrupted, resulting in request latency longer than configured. This is because the timeout mechanism only covers the etcd fetch phase but not the decoding phase.
FIX: Add apiserver.latency.k8s.io/decode-response-object annotation to the audit log to record the decoding time
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/request/webhook_duration.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go
