TITLE: Using server-side-apply for an Ingress failed when updating IngressBackend from port number to port name
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I created an Ingress resource with a port number manually, and then tried to use an Operator with server-side apply to update the resource from a port number to a port name. This failed with the error message "cannot set both port name & port number".

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the port number to be cleared as the operator would take over the ownership of the ServiceBackendPort. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To simulate the behavior in the operator in a most simple example I use `kubectl`:

ingress-v1.yaml:

```
kind: Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: myingress
spec:
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: myservice
      port:
        number: 8443
```

ingress-v2.yaml:

```
kind: Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: myingress
spec:
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: myservice
      port:
        name: http
```

```
kubectl apply -f  ingress-v1.yaml --server-side --field-manager=app-1 --validate=false
kubectl apply -f  ingress-v2.yaml --server-side --field-manager=app-2 --validate=false  --force-con
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the server-side apply merge strategy for the ServiceBackendPort struct was not set to 'atomic'. This caused conflicting updates when one updater set the port number and another tried to set the port name, leading to the error when both fields appeared to be set simultaneously. The lack of atomic merge meant that partial updates conflicted rather than one owner taking exclusive control of the entire port specification.
FIX: Changed how the API server handles updates to `.spec.defaultBackend` of Ingress objects.
Server-side apply now considers `.spec.defaultBackend` to be an atomic struct.  This means that any field-owner who sets values in that struct (they are mutually exclusive) owns the whole struct. For almost all users this change has no impact; for controllers that want to change the default backend port from number to name (or vice-versa), this makes it easier.
FILES: api/openapi-spec/swagger.json, api/openapi-spec/v3/apis__networking.k8s.io__v1_openapi.json, pkg/generated/openapi/zz_generated.openapi.go, staging/src/k8s.io/api/networking/v1/generated.proto, staging/src/k8s.io/api/networking/v1/types.go, staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/internal/internal.go

TITLE: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the ClusterRole for service-account-issuer-discovery defines permissions for nonResourceURLs without trailing slashes, but the OpenAPI spec (swagger.json) documents these URLs with trailing slashes. This mismatch causes RBAC authorization to fail for legally formed requests that append a trailing slash, since the policy does not allow those exact paths.
FIX: Add slash ended urls for service-account-issuer-discovery to match API in swagger

TITLE: [KCCM]: service update while node sync is processing might impact ingress  
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The Kubernetes cloud controller manager uses resource watchers to sync load balancers, a Node/Service watcher. The Node watcher is slower by nature since any Node event will sync all service load balancers on the cluster. The service watcher is quicker since it only syncs the service load balancer which the event relates to. 

How slow a Node sync is will vary on the cluster, i.e: amount of Services of `type: LoadBalancer` and Nodes, but on big clusters with a lot of churn: the time to process one Node sync can be sufficiently slow to have the cache of Nodes go stale w.r.t the actual cluster state. The cache of Nodes is here the resource informer cache. When syncing Nodes the Node control loop will list all Nodes in its cache and then iterate over all Services and sync their load balancers in parallel, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L799-L818

If any Service experiences an update needing a load balancer sync, the Service controller will also list the Nodes in the informer cache, but retrieve a more up-to-date copy, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that the node sets keyed per service were not synchronized between the service and node control loops, causing transient addition and removal of nodes in load balancer backend sets during concurrent node and service syncs. Because lastSyncedNodes was shared globally rather than per service, parallel syncs conflicted, leading to stale node removals after additions.
FIX: KCCM: fix transient node addition + removal caused by #121090 while syncing load balancers on large clusters with a lot of churn
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go, staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/fake/fake.go

SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The traffic should have reached the sidecar container like before the migration.

Create a Pod with a native sidecar container (initContainer) with a named port, as well as a Kubernetes Service using that named port as its targetPort. This port is not listed in the Endpoint.

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sidecar-ports
  labels:

spec:
  containers:
  - image: bloomberg/goldpinger:3.10.1

TITLE: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.


### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

1.27+

### Cloud provider

<details>
N/A
</details>

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

# On Windows:
C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

```

</details>

### Install tools

<details>

</details>

ROOT CAUSE: The backoff delay calculation for recreating pods in a Job controller excluded pods whose failures matched an 'Ignore' rule in the Job's failure policy. TITLE: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an intern
ROOT CAUSE: The job controller initiates creation of replacement pods immediately upon noticing a pod deletion without waiting for the original pod to fully terminate. This premature creation can lead to multiple pods running concurrently when parallelism is set to 1, violating users' expectations and causing application failures. The controller did not implement a mechanism to delay pod creation until the pod state was confirmed as terminated.

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu


ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller's back-off logic was coupled with the workqueue's back-off mechanism, causing rapid rescheduling of failed pods without proper exponential delay. This coupling meant multiple pod failures within a reconciliation cycle did not properly aggregate back-off delays, resulting in retries being scheduled too frequently and ignoring exponential backoff requirements.
FIX: The job controller back-off logic is now decoupled from workqueue. In case of parallelism > 1, if there are multiple new failures in a reconciliation cycle, all the failures are taken into account to compute the back-off. Previously, the back-off kicked in for all types of failures; with this change, only pod failures are taken into account. If the back-off limits exceeds, the job is marked as failed immediately; before this change, the job is marked as failed in the next back-off.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The root cause is that the kubelet suppression logic is ineffective because it always sees at least one non-error SyncResult (ConfigPodSandbox) with nil error. This causes backoff errors from container start failures to propagate as errors and cause the pod worker to immediately requeue the pod with a fixed short delay (10s), instead of respecting the intended exponential backoff timing. This leads to rapid immediate retries, log spam, and unnecessary work. The defect lies in inadequate error aggregation and propagation coordination between syncPod and podWorkers components.

claims.text: The error suppression logic in pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go's syncPod method is flawed because it tests whether all SyncResults errors are backoff errors, but there is always a non-error SyncResult (ConfigPodSandbox) with nil error, causing suppression to never trigger and backoff errors to propagate as actual errors.

The pod worker in pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go immediately requeues pods with a 10s backoff whenever syncPod returns any error, including backoff errors, causing immediate retries instead of respecting longer exponential backoff periods.

The kuberuntime_manager's syncPod propagates backoff errors from starting containers, which combined with the flawed suppression logic in kubelet.go, results in backoff errors causing immediate pod requeueing.

TITLE: CRD validation allows invalid CABundles that will fail setting up handlers
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

A CRDs with an invalid conversion webhook CABundle failed to serve requests not requiring conversion.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since creating cr-1.yaml doesn't require conversion, I would have expected either:

1. An error response when attempting to create/update the CRD with an invalid CABundle
2. Only an error when conversion is required to server a request

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


Create a mult-version CRD with a conversion webhook configured with an invalid CABundle:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: replicant.stable.example.com
spec:
  group: stable.example.com
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                myfield:
                  type: integer
    - name: v2
      served: true
      storage: false
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              ty
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the CRD validation logic allowed invalid or non-PEM-encoded CABundles to be accepted when creating or updating CustomResourceDefinitions. This caused failures later when setting up conversion webhook handlers, which expect a valid CA certificate bundle for secure communication. Without proper validation at CRD creation time, invalid CABundles lead to internal errors and prevented serving requests properly.
FIX: CustomResourceDefinition objects created with non-empty `caBundle` fields which are invalid or do not contain any certificates will not appear in discovery or serve endpoints until a valid `caBundle` is provided. Updates to CustomResourceDefinition are no longer allowed to transition a valid `caBundle` field to an invalid `caBundle` field, because this breaks serving of the existing CustomResourceDefinition.

goroutine 883 [running]:
k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime.logPanic({0x3de2d20?, 0x6fc0d90})
	/go/src/kubernetes/vendor/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime/runtime.go:75 +0x85
k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime.HandleCrash({0x0, 0x0, 0x0?})

	/usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:914 +0x21f

	/go/src/kubernetes/pkg/
ROOT CAUSE: The kubelet code did not handle the case where the Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver returns a nil pointer for the NodePrepareResources or NodeUnprepareResources response. Because protobuf encoding can omit empty objects leading to nil pointers, this caused a nil pointer dereference panic in the kubelet.

diagnosis.root_cause: The crash occurs because the type-checking logic in kube-controller-manager's ValidatingAdmissionPolicy controller does not correctly handle a CRD field defined as type=object with additionalProperties=true in the policy's matchConstraints. The type-checking code assumes stricter schema definitions and panics when encountering the dynamic arbitrary fields permitted by additionalProperties: true, lacking proper nil or boundary checks for this structure.

claims.text: The panic happens during type-checking the matchConstraints ResourceRules in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy when it encounters a CRD field with type=object and additionalProperties=true, as reported in the ticket.

The typechecking.go file extracts GVKs from matchConstraints ResourceRules but does not handle object properties with additionalProperties:true properly, potentially causing a crash downstream when type-checking those schemas.

TITLE: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the fi
ROOT CAUSE: The scheduler's cache entries for pod-to-node assignments expire after a fixed 30-second timeout. When the API server is under heavy load and the bind operation takes longer than 30s, the cache prematurely removes the assignment. This causes the scheduler to lose track of the actual binding state, leading it to incorrectly schedule another pod onto the same node, resulting in race conditions on large clusters.
FIX: Remove TTL for scheduler cache to resolve the race condition when Cac…
FILES: pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go, pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go

TITLE: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L519-L543
4.  Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

```
Jul 25 1
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is a concurrency race in kubelet's device manager when allocating GPU devices to pods. The mutex guarding the allocated devices map is unlocked while calling out to device plugins, allowing concurrent updates and leading to inconsistent or nil map values. This causes the allocation function to panic due to nil map assignments when multiple GPU-using pods are created or deleted concurrently.
FIX: Fix kubelet panic when allocate resource for pod.
FILES: pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go, pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager_test.go

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

claims.text: Concurrent creation and deletion of pods with emptyDir and the feature gate LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring enabled triggers concurrent calls to emptyDir.teardownDefault, which invokes fsquota.ClearQuota to clear filesystem quotas.

The concurrent map writes error occurs because multiple goroutines call ClearQuota concurrently without sufficient synchronization around all accesses to shared maps, leading to concurrent mutations.

TITLE: Conntrack cleaning happens before network programming endpoints
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Currently kube-proxy efficiently cleans all stale conntrack entries preventing traffic black holing for deleted endpoints, but there can be some corner cases when conntrack cleaning happens before programming the network leaving a small window in which if any packet arrives will back-hole the traffic.

The corner case:
Taking a simple case of load-balancer service backed by a deployment with single replica, on deleting the pod(gracefully), I observed two **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocations:
1.  First one with EndpointConditions.Ready as false
2. EndpointSlice was cleared for the pod 

The conntrack flow for this case:
1. After processing the first **OnEndpointSliceUpdate** invocation **EndpointsMap** will still have entries for the pod as endpoint still exists, though not in ready state so proxier won't program deletion of endpoint from the data path. But the endpoint IP will be picked for conntrack cleaning as new endpoint != old endpoint because of the not ready condition.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288eda15da1724989f3f7dec9f3512d6/pkg/proxy/endpoints.go#L423-L436
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e915c4288e
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because the conntrack cleaning logic considers endpoint readiness changes as an indication to clean stale connections before the network datapath has been updated to reflect those changes. This causes a timing window where conntrack entries are cleaned ahead of actual network programming, potentially blackholing traffic.
FIX: Fix stale conntrack flow detection logic
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier_test.go, pkg/proxy/types.go

TITLE: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersRe
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by a race condition in kube-proxy's iptables mode partial sync logic, where `syncProxyRules` made separate calls to check for pending updates and then apply them. Since the change trackers use their own mutexes independent from the proxier's, a new event could be processed between these calls, leading to inconsistent state and some endpoint updates being missed.
FIX: Fixes a race condition in the iptables mode of kube-proxy in 1.27 and later
that could result in some updates getting lost (e.g., when a service gets a
new endpoint, the rules for the new endpoint might not be added until
much later).
FILES: pkg/proxy/endpoints.go, pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go, pkg/proxy/endpointslicecache.go, pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go, pkg/proxy/service.go, pkg/proxy/service_test.go

AKS had a customer report repeated issues in their clusters where:

2. Envoy c-ares DNS client would send repeated DNS queries to the kube-dns service VIP from the same src IP address, creating a UDP conntrack entry to the svc VIP and keeping it alive. For example, with kube-dns svc VIP 192.168.0.10, conntrack showed:

Issue occurred only in clusters with many services and endpoints (~10k services and ~6k endpoints). However, the customer has seen this issue repeatedly for months, about 1-5 times per week across their clusters.

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy code to delete stale UDP conntrack entries should have de
ROOT CAUSE: Kube-proxy was marking its initialization as complete before all service and endpointslice updates had been fully processed and delivered. This led to incomplete service state, causing transient removal of service rules and failure to clean up stale UDP conntrack entries.

This is because the cleanupAllPolicies method does not properly synchronize RemoteEndpoints deletion when multiple services share endpoints, causing delayed or skipped cleanup.

### What happened?

TITLE: removeMissingExtendedResources() did not remove unknown extension resources from InitContainer
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The function removeMissingExtendedResources() located at pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/predicate.go:217, is designed to remove any extended resources from a container’s requests that are not found in nodeInfo.Allocatable before the pod is admitted. This is necessary to support cluster-level resources, which are extended resources that are unknown to nodes.
However, this function only removes missingExtendedResources from the container’s requests, and does not process the requests of initContainers. This could lead to issues, as initContainers might request resources that do not exist on the node, which could result in the pod failing to be admitted or other unforeseen issues. As such, it may be necessary to refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### What did you expect to happen?

Refine the removeMissingExtendedResources() function to also handle initContainer’s requests.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod that requests cluster-level extended resources in both the container and InitContainer.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes versi
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug was that the removeMissingExtendedResources() function was incomplete in its processing scope; it only sanitized the extended resource requests of regular containers but neglected to perform the same cleanup for initContainers. Since initContainers can also request extended resources unknown to the node, this omission led to potential resource mismatches and pod admission failures.
FIX: Remove missing extended resources from init containers

diagnosis.root_cause: The root cause is that the controller handling StatefulSets in Kubernetes versions prior to 1.34 included a `creationTimestamp: null` field in the `spec.template.metadata` of the pod template, which was removed in v1.34. This removal causes the controller to detect spurious differences in the StatefulSet spec during upgrade, triggering unnecessary rollouts of pods. Thus, the bug happens because the StatefulSet controller's comparison logic or patching mechanism detects a change due to removal of a previously ignored `creationTimestamp: null` field in pod template metadata, causing pods to be replaced unnecessarily.

claims.text: The ticket states that the upgrade from 1.33 to 1.34 removes the field `creationTimestamp: null` inside spec.template.metadata, which leads to spurious pod rollouts of StatefulSets, implying that the removal of this field causes the controller to detect differences triggering re-creation of pods.

The removal of the `creationTimestamp: null` field in pod template metadata changes the spec seen by the StatefulSet controller, causing it to incorrectly consider the pod template changed and to trigger a rollout even though the actual pod spec is effectively the same.

The StatefulSet controller source in `pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go` is involved in managing StatefulSets lifecycle and likely performs the spec reconciliation and equality checks responsible for detecting pod template changes and initiating rollouts.

TITLE: The event handlers of job controller are slow
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The event handlers in job controller are much slower than other controllers. It can cause the ring buffer in the processorListener to grow unbounded when the job churn is high enough.
The processing logic in the job controller events handler appears to be more complicated than other controllers. e.g. in [updateJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L464-L504), it invokes function `cleanupPodFinalizers` that lists the pods matching some selectors and the enqueue them to another queue. Similarly in [deleteJob](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dbc2b0a5c7acc349ea71a14e49913661eaf708d2/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L508-L524).

I added some instrumenting code to understand the latency of each event handler.
For job controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.080 ms
job update event handler: 3.075 ms
job delete event handler: 3.076 ms
pod add event handler: 0.136 ms
pod update event handler: 0.709 ms
pod delete event handler: 0.405 ms

For ttl-after-completion controller P99:
job add event handler: 0.0065 ms
job update event handler: 0.024 ms

T
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the slowness is that the job controller's event handlers perform complex and expensive operations directly within the event handler methods, such as listing pods and enqueuing them, instead of deferring such processing to the controller's main reconcile loop. This design leads to high latency and potential buildup of events, especially under high job churn.
FIX: Improve performance of the job controller when handling job update events.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: CronJob gets stuck when jobs quota is reached
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We (in Booking.com) run CronJobs in Kubernetes clusters with ResourceQuota's defined. When quota for # of jobs is reached we observed that CronJobs:
1. stop scheduling new jobs (because quota is reached),
2. don't clean the old jobs (despite # of jobs > history allows and the fact that it would unblock the CronJob new Jobs). 

The only way to progress is to remove enough Jobs to make room for a new Job in namespace quota. When we do that manually, the CronJob kicks in.

The workaround we found around the internet is to specify `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` for the job template. But it's not ideal as it's not a history-based limit, but a time-based limit, and often you want to have the last N jobs to be around for debugging.

### What did you expect to happen?

When jobs quota is reached and # of cronjob jobs exceeds specified the history limit, these jobs are deleted giving room for new jobs to run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: job-quota
  namespace: default
spec:
  hard:
    count/jobs.batch: "1"
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metad
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because when the cronjob controller failed to create a new Job due to hitting the resource quota limit, it aborted the iteration early without performing cleanup of old finished Jobs. This prevented the controller from deleting obsolete Jobs to free quota, causing a deadlock where new Jobs could never be scheduled.
FIX: Fixed an issue where a CronJob could fail to clean up Jobs when the ResourceQuota for Jobs had been reached.
FILES: pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go, pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2_test.go

TITLE: Job controller reports the count of ready pods with unnecessary delay
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminat
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the Job controller counts ready pods only among the currently active pods during deletion, but since the number of active pods updates asynchronously and may decrease after the count was made, the ready pod count does not get updated promptly to reflect pods that are terminating or deleted. This lag causes stale ready counts until the cache refreshes.
FIX: Now the .status.ready field is tracked faster when active Pods are deleted, specifically when Job is failed, gets suspended or has too many active pods
FILES: pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go

TITLE: Kubernetes Jobs API rapid-fire scheduling doesnt honor exponential backoff characteristics
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

# Problem

The job controller appears to "rapidly reschedule" several pods at the same time (without backing off) which ultimately appears almost like a batch or gang scheduling workflow.  

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu


ROOT CAUSE: The Job controller's back-off logic was coupled with the workqueue's back-off mechanism, causing rapid rescheduling of failed pods without proper exponential delay. This coupling meant multiple pod failures within a reconciliation cycle did not properly aggregate back-off delays, resulting in retries being scheduled too frequently and ignoring exponential backoff requirements.
FIX: The job controller back-off logic is now decoupled from workqueue. In case of parallelism > 1, if there are multiple new failures in a reconciliation cycle, all the failures are taken into account to compute the back-off. Previously, the back-off kicked in for all types of failures; with this change, only pod failures are taken into account. If the back-off limits exceeds, the job is marked as failed immediately; before this change, the job is marked as failed in the next back-off.
FILES: pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils.go, pkg/controller/job/backoff_utils_test.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go, pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go, test/integration/job/job_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug arises because the Job controller unconditionally resets the Job's status.StartTime to the current time whenever a suspended Job is resumed. The validation logic forbids changing status.StartTime for unsuspended Jobs once it is set, causing the controller's update request to be rejected and logged as an error. The controller does not distinguish between a fresh resume and an ongoing unsuspended Job, so it attempts to update StartTime repeatedly, triggering the validation error.

claims.text: The job controller resets status.StartTime to the current time every time a suspended Job is resumed without checking if the Job was already unsuspended, causing updates to status.StartTime on unsuspended Jobs.
The validation logic forbids changing status.StartTime for unsuspended Jobs from one non-nil value to another, triggering errors when the controller attempts to update StartTime on resume.
The error message in the job controller logs and observed update request indicate that status.StartTime is updated to a new time on resuming the Job, leading to an invalid status update error.

TITLE: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from t
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause is that when a Pod has its spec.nodeName field set (indicating it is pre-assigned to a specific node), the Dynamic Resources scheduler plugin is bypassed and does not run. Since this plugin is responsible for managing resource claims and reservations, bypassing it leads to the pod being rejected or failing to run because its resource claims are not properly allocated or reserved. This limitation arises because the scheduler plugin is skipped when the pod is pre-scheduled, preventing the dynamic resource allocation logic from executing.
FIX: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
FILES: cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/core.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go, pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller_test.go, plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/controller_policy.go, staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/controller/controller.go, test/e2e/dra/dra.go, test/e2e/dra/test-driver/app/controller.go, test/integration/util/util.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the kubelet DRA manager matches container resource claims against prepared resource claims by comparing the container's claim.Name, which is from the pod spec, to claimInfo.ClaimName, which is the actual resource claim object's name. For resource claims created via claim templates, these names differ, causing the matching logic to fail and preventing health statuses from being reported for those claims.

claims.text: The condition `if cClaim.Name == claimInfo.ClaimName` in pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go incorrectly compares the pod spec claim name (container resource claim name) with the actual resource claim object's name, which differ for claims created from templates, causing the health status not to be associated with the container's claims.

Logs show that the kubelet fails to find matching resource claims in the container spec for claims created from resource claim templates, confirming that the matching logic does not handle template-generated claim names correctly.

TITLE: `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I’m seeing some odd behavior with 1.28.2 that was not present in earlier releases, with regards to aggregated api services. It appears that the `poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller` is now blocking the apiserver from becoming ready for 1 minute, if discovery for an aggregated apiservice is not available when the apiserver is started. Note that this only happens if the apiservice is marked available when the apiserver is started; if it is unavailable at startup (Available status: false), or the service has no endpoints, the health check does not block and readyz returns `ok` without delay.

I am seeing this behavior in 1.28.1 and 1.28.2, but not v1.27.6 or v1.27.5

### What did you expect to happen?

apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy metrics-server to a Kubernetes cluster
2. Wait for api registration for `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` to complete (Available status is `true`).
3. Kill the kubelet and pods on the node hosting the metrics-server pod, such that the metrics-server service continues to show available endpoints, but the endpoint is 
ROOT CAUSE: The bug was caused by the AddUpdateAPIService function simultaneously adding and updating the APIService spec during startup, rather than deferring the spec update to be handled asynchronously by the controller. This synchronous update caused race conditions and health check blocking when discovery failed, leading to readiness delays.
FIX: Fix regression with adding aggregated apiservices panicking and affected health check introduced in release v1.28.0

TITLE: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

TITLE: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071128Z Waiting for caches to sync for crd-autoregister
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.270943Z Caches are synced for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.471323Z Caches are synced for crd-autoregister
```

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02
ROOT CAUSE: The server startup code incorrectly detects whether the CustomResourceDefinitions (CRD) API is enabled by checking the wrong condition or using improper logic. As a result, the autoregister controller proceeds to reconcile and delete APIService objects before the CRD controller has synced, causing a race condition where APIs for existing CRDs are mistakenly deleted at startup.
FIX: Fixes a bug at kube-apiserver start where APIService objects for custom resources could be deleted and recreated.
FILES: cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go, cmd/kube-apiserver/app/testing/testserver.go, test/integration/examples/apiserver_test.go

TITLE: [Bug] Missing constraint and validation for label selector's values
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Hello,
There are some [constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set) that label selector's `values` need to conform:
>* must be 63 characters or less (can be empty),
>* unless empty, must begin and end with an alphanumeric character ([a-z0-9A-Z]),
>* could contain dashes (-), underscores (_), dots (.), and alphanumerics between.

Every label selctor's `values` will be checked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e5ba5cd2b0d3bddd4a0393b98fde14960f31a33c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L166C1-L175C2), and when values is not conforming these constraints, an error will be returned.

`nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms.matchExpressions.values` also needs to conform these constraints (because `matchExpressions` will be parsed as a label selector), but cccording to the [concept documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#operators) and the [API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.31/#nodeselectorrequirement-v1-core), 
ROOT CAUSE: The underlying cause is that the system did not validate the values in NodeSelectorRequirement against label value constraints during pod creation. This lack of validation allowed invalid strings to be accepted, leading to parse errors during scheduling and causing the scheduler to reject the node selector terms silently without warning the user.
FIX: kubenetes starts validating NodeSelectorRequirement's values when creating pods.
FILES: pkg/api/node/util.go, pkg/api/persistentvolume/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util.go, pkg/api/pod/util_test.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings.go, pkg/api/pod/warnings_test.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers.go, pkg/apis/core/helper/helpers_test.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go, pkg/apis/core/validation/validation_test.go

TITLE: kube-proxy in LocalModeNodeCIDR mode may cache stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is recreated
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If `LocalModeNodeCIDR` is true, kube-proxy reads the `Node.PodCIDR` value and uses it to determine whether or not traffic is local to the Node.

In certain cases (e.g. when kube-proxy runs before the Node information has been completely updated), it is possible for kube-proxy to read and store a stale `PodCIDR` value. This will cause kube-proxy to route traffic incorrectly as the local traffic determination is no longer correct.

Note: PodCIDR is immutable once set but it is possible to delete and recreate the Node object to get into this state. (yes, this can happen)



### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should detect this state and reconfigure/restart with the newly updated `PodCIDR`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Recreate the Node object with a different PodCIDR after kube-proxy has started on the Node.

### Kubernetes version

Impacts all current versions that support `LocalModeNodeCIDR`

### Cloud provider

<details>
Observed for GCE preemptible/spot VMs, but is a generic problem.
</details>
ROOT CAUSE: kube-proxy reads the Node object's PodCIDR at startup and caches it, but does not update this cached PodCIDR when the Node object is deleted and recreated with a different PodCIDR. Therefore, kube-proxy continues to use the stale PodCIDR for local traffic determination, causing incorrect routing.
FIX: kube-proxy, will restart in case it detects that the Node assigned pod.Spec.PodCIDRs have changed
FILES: cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_others.go, cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_others_test.go, pkg/proxy/node.go, pkg/proxy/node_test.go, pkg/proxy/topology.go, pkg/proxy/topology_test.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the kubelet uses stale node label data from its informer cache to validate node affinity, leading to wrongful pod rejections. This stale cache is not updated in real-time, causing the kubelet's node affinity check to be out-of-sync with the scheduler's more current view. This discrepancy arises from the kubelet relying solely on informer data without synchronous fallback fetches to the API server when node affinity validation fails.

claims.text: The kubelet rejects pods due to stale informer data not reflecting recent node label updates which the scheduler sees, leading to node affinity validation failures on kubelet.

The proposed fix involves synchronous fetching of the node object from the API server when node affinity errors occur, indicating the problem stems from informer cache staleness and lack of timely updates.
The scheduling cache code compares resourceVersions to detect newer node data, which is relevant to the suggested isNewer check for node data freshness in the kubelet fix.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because the server-side-apply managedFields merging logic enforces a strict equality of patch and storage versions (e.g., v1beta1 vs v1) during status subresource updates. When the status is updated via a different API version than the storage version, the version check fails and managedFields merging is skipped or misapplied, leading to managedFields being wiped. The ticket reproduces the bug by creating a CRD with multiple versions (v1beta1 and v1) and updating the status subresource with a different version than the storage version, which causes managedFields to be wiped unexpectedly.

TITLE: Transient Driver Registration on the CSINode can Result in Missed NodeUnstageVolume RPCs During Pod Migration
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In `unmountDetachDevices` (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03126c5465879491be33d5064e6f6f1c4ff2a276/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L279-L316)) we have the following code that will ultimately dispatch `NodeUnstageVolume` RPCs to the underlying CSI plugin.

Here is a pseudo-code representation of the current logic:

```
function unmountDetachDevices
	for all unmounted volumes in ASoW
		if volume not in DSoW &&
		   not operation pending on volume
			if device is mounted globally or
			   device is mounted uncertain
				Case A:
				unmount device
				(this will kick off the NodeUnstageVolume RPC; we want to be here)
			else
				Case B:
				just remove volume from ASoW
				(general badness since we don't issue a NodeUnstageVolume RPC)
```

In our testbeds, we have observed a number of occurrences where we fall into `Case B` when the CSI Node plugin for a particular driver is being bounced, which leads to the volumemanager failing to dispatch the `NodeUnstageVolume` RPC. If the pod migrates to another node, this will leave behind a Zombie LUN in our testbeds (we're using iSCSI).

A Zombie LUN can and often does resu
ROOT CAUSE: The CSI attacher treats the absence of the CSI driver during a NodeStageVolume call as a final error, transitioning volume devices from uncertain to unmounted state prematurely. This causes unmountDetachDevices logic to skip issuing NodeUnstageVolume RPCs, potentially leaving volumes in a zombie state. The root cause is misclassification of a missing CSI driver error as final rather than transient, leading to incorrect device state transitions and missed cleanup calls.
FIX: Retry NodeStageVolume calls if CSI node driver is not running

2. Shutdown the node while pod was running.
3. Wait for node to go `NotReady` and pod to switch to `Terminating` state.

TITLE: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, chec
ROOT CAUSE: The volume_manager's podWorker calls WaitForUnmount asynchronously. If the final asynchronous call happens after the populator has cleaned up its resources, a pod UID is added to the processedPods map but the populator no longer tracks that pod. This pod entry then remains in processedPods indefinitely because the cleanup code only processes pods currently tracked by the volume_manager's internal cache.
FIX: Fix memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

See steps to reproduce below, it's quite a complex condition. It happens when a pod is restarted, a CSI driver "busy" (i.e. times out) + KCM restarted at a wrong time.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods start just fine.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


1. Create a Pod that uses an attachable CSI volume.
2. Delete the Pod. Make sure it unmounts successfully, but any `ControllerUnpublish` fails with a transient error, such as timeout. The external attacher continues to detach the volume at this point.
3. Stop kube-controller-manager (KCM) and start a new one. Wait for any leader election etc - it's important for the new KCM to populate A/D controller with no pod using the detaching volume. Let the A/D controller to observe detach error.
4. Create
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because after a failed detach attempt, the attach/detach controller incorrectly marks the volume as fully attached instead of uncertain. This causes Kubernetes to believe the volume is attached when it might still be detaching, leading to Pod mounting attempts on volumes that are not truly attached. Additionally, after KCM restart, volumes without Pods are marked as uncertain but also incorrectly as attached in the actual state of the node, which prevents proper re-attachment and causes Pods to get stuck during container creation.

TITLE: In-tree vSphere volumes are not detached after KCM restart
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I am enabling CSI migration on a vSphere cluster. A node was fully drained, all its Pods are deleted, but just before KCM detaches in-tree vSphere volume volumes from it, KCM restarts. A new KCM starts, sees attached volumes in `node.status.volumesAttached` that are not needed by any Pod on the node and calls vSphere in-tree volume plugin `Detach()`.

The in-tree vSphere volume plugin + cloud provider marks the volume as detached right away, without reaching to vCenter API. The volume remains attached forever.

I don't think it's related to CSI migration, IMO a regular node drain + KCM restart at the same time can cause the same issue.

KCM logs:

```
I0404 14:58:42.423920       1 operation_generator.go:1637] Verified volume is safe to detach for volume "nil" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/vsphere-volume/[WorkloadDatastore] 8b577f5f-ea23-1e5e-bac9-0693938623e5/_029e/_0040/7f718f6c06a84cff86e254dfcd150be1.vmdk") on node "jsafrane-rdpmz-worker-ps6qk" 
I0404 14:58:42.423986       1 nodemanager.go:359] No VM found for node "jsafrane-rdpmz-worker-ps6qk". Initiating rediscovery.
E0404 14:58:42.434007       1 nodemanager.go:362] Error "No VM found" node info fo
ROOT CAUSE: The vSphere cloud provider maintains an internal cache of nodes using informer events that are asynchronous. During kube-controller-manager startup, this cache may not yet be fully populated when volume detach operations occur. As a result, the cloud provider cannot find the node in its cache, mistakenly assumes the volume is detached, and skips calling the vCenter API to detach the volume. This causes the volume to remain indefinitely attached in vCenter.
FIX: Fixed vSphere cloud provider not to skip detach volumes from nodes at kube-controller-startup.
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/nodemanager.go, staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/nodemanager_test.go, staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/vsphere/vsphere.go

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because when the csi-node-plugin Pod is deleted, the driver entry in the CSINode object is removed. During this period, the kube-scheduler's NodeVolumeLimits plugin fails to find any volume limits for the node's CSI driver in the CSINode object and incorrectly assumes there are no limits, allowing scheduling beyond the node's actual attachable volume count. This vulnerability arises because the NodeVolumeLimits plugin treats missing volume limit information as an absence of limits, instead of rejecting scheduling in the absence of reliable driver data.

claims.text: The NodeVolumeLimits plugin's Filter function allows scheduling if no volume limits are found on the CSINode object, as evidenced by the code returning nil when getVolumeLimits returns an empty map, which corresponds exactly to the bug scenario where CSINode driver info is temporarily missing during csi-node-plugin Pod deletion.

Deletion of csi-node-plugin Pod causes the driver section to be removed from CSINode objects, removing volume limit information temporarily until the Pod restarts, leading to scheduler allowing Pods to be scheduled beyond limits.

TITLE: False MountVolume.NodeExpandVolume failure warning message for readOnly pods

It seems like this message is being triggered from here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L2079


But we never did an expand volume call, so we should not be seeing warning message. It can be confusing to see this warning message.

ROOT CAUSE: The code incorrectly logs a 'FileSystemResizeFailed' warning when a pod mounts a volume in read-only mode, even though no volume expansion was actually attempted. TITLE: NewVolumeManagerReconstruction: Volumes are reported as unmounted after reboot
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Kubernetes 1.27 with `NewVolumeManagerReconstruction` feature gate **enabled** and `SELinuxMountReadWriteOncePod` **disabled**, a rebooted node is not able to re-start pods that were running there before the reboot.

The node reports in Pod events:

```
Warning  FailedMount             2m4s (x5 over 11m)  kubelet                  Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[myvol], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[]: timed out waiting for the condition
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The Pod should start just fine.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On Kubernetes 1.27:
1. Enable NewVolumeManagerReconstruction feature gate.
2. Run a StatefulSet that uses a volume.
3. Force-reboot the node which runs the StatefulSet Pod.

### Anything else we need to know?

The reason is that kubelet's VolumeManager reconstructs the volume as _uncertain_ during startup and it uses a provisional _outer volume name_ for it, because it has not seen the API server and Pods in it yet. This provisional volume ID is then used in ActualStateOfWorld forever.

While kubelet _does_ mount the volume after reboo
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurs because during kubelet startup with the NewVolumeManagerReconstruction feature gate enabled and SELinuxMountReadWriteOncePod disabled, volumes are reconstructed with a provisional outer volume name before the Pod and API server state is synced. This provisional volume ID is stored indefinitely and used in ActualStateOfWorld, so kubelet cannot correlate the volume with the Pod's expected volume name, causing Pod restart failures after node reboot.
FIX: Fix pod restart after node reboot when NewVolumeManagerReconstruction feature gate is enabled and SELinuxMountReadWriteOncePod disabled

claims.text: The SELinux warning controller reports conflicting SELinux labels for pods that are in Failed or Succeeded phases although these pods no longer hold mounted volumes because kubelet unmounts those by default after pod termination.

TITLE: sched: CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins not always injected into cycleState
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

In k8s 1.27, scheduler introduced a new "short circuit" semantics in PreFilter to bypass a Pod quickly. A change introduced here is it relies on that plugin to be stored in `CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins`, which makes sense as what it was explained [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114125/files#r1062646736).

However, the `SkipFilterPlugins` info, although is populated upon each plugin's PreFilter invocation, is not injected into `CycleState` when some PreFilter returns unschedulable:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L655-L661

So think about this workflow:

- pluginA returns Skip in its PreFilter
- pluginB return Unschedulable in its PreFilter
- note: pluginA is not included in `CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins` due to aforementioned bug
- a Pod is claimed as unschedulable (failed by pluginB)
- during PostFilter, it's **supposed** to bypass pluginA's PreEnqueueExtension's AddPod/RemovePod, but it doesn't
- calling a "skipped" Plugin's AddPod/RemovePod during preemption, sometimes will abort the whole preemption as the logic tries to rea
ROOT CAUSE: The bug happened because the scheduler framework did not properly inject the SkipFilterPlugins information into the CycleState when a PreFilter plugin returned Unschedulable. As a result, during PostFilter, plugins that relied on CycleState.SkipFilterPlugins to know which plugins to skip could fail or behave incorrectly because this information was missing.
FIX: Fixed a 1.27 scheduling regression that PostFilter plugin may not function if previous PreFilter plugins return Skip
FILES: pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go, pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework_test.go, test/integration/scheduler/preemption/preemption_test.go

TITLE: wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke condition function at least once
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Calling wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke the passed condition function if context has already been cancelled.


### What did you expect to happen?

wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true should invoke the passed condition function at least once even if context has already been cancelled as wait.PollUntilContextCancel documentation says:

> If immediate is true, condition will be invoked before waiting and guarantees that condition is invoked at least once, regardless of whether the context has been cancelled.

Note that wait.PollUntilContextTimeout wraps wait.PollUntilContextCancel, so the above should be applied to wait.PollUntilContextTimeout as well.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import (
        "context"
        "time"

        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

func main() {
        err := wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second, 0, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) {
                return true, nil
        })
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
}
```

This program pan
ROOT CAUSE: The implementation of wait.PollUntilContextTimeout immediately checks the context for cancellation before executing the condition function. This causes the condition function to never be called if the context is already cancelled, violating the API contract that the condition must be called at least once when immediate=true.
FIX: wait.PollUntilContextTimeout function, if immediate is true, the condition will be invoked before waiting and guarantees that the condition is invoked at least once, regardless of whether the context has been cancelled.
FILES: staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait/loop.go, staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait/loop_test.go

TITLE: When PreFilter's PreFilterResult filter out some Nodes, unschedulable plugin isn't registered for those plugins
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

2. FilterA filters out NodeA.

### What did you expect to happen?

2. FilterA filters out NodeA.

TITLE: "Connection reset by peer" due to invalid conntrack packets
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

When packets with sequence number out-of-window arrived k8s node, conntrack marked them as INVALID. kube-proxy will ignore them, without rewriting DNAT. However, there is no corresponding session link on the host, and the host sends a reset packet, causing the session link to be interrupted

### What did you expect to happen?

connection not reset

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839

### Anything else we need to know?

This problem can be solved by command：
iptables -t filter -I INPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate INVALID -j DROP

Similar issue:https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74839
But this issue "drop" is placed on the forward chain, our scenario needs to be placed on the input chain.

### Kubernetes version


$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.0", GitCommit:"c2b5237ccd9c0f1d600d3072634ca66cefdf272f", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-08-04T18:03:20Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.0", GitCommit
ROOT CAUSE: The bug occurred because kube-proxy installed an iptables rule that unconditionally dropped packets with an INVALID conntrack state. In some network scenarios, such as nodes with multihoming, legitimate traffic can be mistakenly marked as INVALID by conntrack. Dropping such packets causes unexpected connection resets because kube-proxy does not rewrite DNAT for them. The fix was to make kube-proxy conditionally install these DROP rules only if the system-wide nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal setting is not set, avoiding disruptions from misclassified INVALID packets.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug happens because the conntrack cleanup logic in kube-proxy changed after v1.32 from efficient batch deletion using the `conntrack -D` command to a slower method of deleting conntrack entries one-by-one using netlink API calls. This per-entry deletion iterates through all matching entries, sending individual netlink delete requests, resulting in severe performance degradation when dealing with large numbers of entries (e.g., >140k), causing prolonged cleanup times that block rule synchronization and lead to service outages.

claims.text: After Kubernetes v1.32, kube-proxy replaced batch conntrack entry deletion via the `conntrack -D` command with individual deletion using netlink API, as described in the ticket.
The current implementation of CleanStaleEntries in pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go lists all conntrack entries then deletes stale entries individually via ClearEntries.
ClearEntries in pkg/proxy/conntrack/conntrack.go calls ConntrackDeleteFilters, which deletes each conntrack entry one by one by making separate netlink API calls, causing slow cleanup.

This per-entry deletion approach is low-efficiency and results in cleanup times increasing from under a second before v1.32 to several minutes in v1.33 and above when many entries exist, leading to blocking of syncProxyRules and service access issues during cleanup periods.

TITLE:  kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as al
ROOT CAUSE: The root cause of the bug is that the iptables rule ordering in the KUBE-IPVS-FILTER chain wrongly rejected packets to healthCheckNodePorts on loadBalancer IPs, due to a restrictive rule introduced to reject new connections to IPVS IPs except for known service IPs. This rule blocked healthcheck traffic from GCP to the node ports for health checking, causing probes to fail. The healthCheckNodePort accept rule was missing in the iptables filter chain prior to the rejecting rule, causing legitimate healthcheck traffic to be dropped.

TITLE: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue
ROOT CAUSE: The kube-proxy component lacked a properly configured --nodeport-addresses setting in a dual-stack environment, causing it to listen on all IP interfaces (0.0.0.0 and ::) by default. This results in healthCheckNodePort binding to all zeros (wildcard address) instead of a node's specific IP, because the code defaults to listening on all addresses if no specific nodeport address ranges are configured.
FIX: The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)

diagnosis.root_cause: The bug occurs because kube-proxy's EndpointSet and EndpointSliceCache deduplication logic uses endpoint hash keys that do not distinguish endpoints adequately when two endpoints have the same IP but differ in terminating status. This causes terminating endpoints to overwrite or be preferred over running endpoints when building endpoint sets, leading kube-proxy to consider only terminating endpoints and therefore not generate iptables rules for the actual running pods.

claims.text: The EndpointSet.Insert method replaces endpoints based on the hashEndpoint key unconditionally, so a terminating endpoint can overwrite a running endpoint with the same IP, leading to loss of the running endpoint in the set.

The EndpointSliceCache.addEndpoints method also deduplicates endpoints by a string key without properly considering terminating conditions, which can cause only the terminating endpoint to be added and the running endpoint ignored.

Because kube-proxy does not see the running endpoint, it generates no iptables rules for the service IP, causing connectivity to fail as observed in the live example with two pods sharing an IP but different termination states.

TITLE: Server-side apply has trouble with empty map
SYMPTOM: ### What happened?

Every time I server-side apply a `Deployment` with `spec.template.metadata.annotations: {}`, the `resourceVersion` updates. Nothing about my manifest changes between applies; if I map `annotations` to the empty map, `kubectl apply --server-side` the same manifest updates the `resourceVersion`. With client-side apply, the `resourceVersion` stays the same as long as my manifest remains constant, even if `annotations: {}`.

I read in #70281 that Kubernetes should treat absent keys, empty values (in this case, an empty map), and `null` values the same. I observe that leaving the `annotations` key out and `annotations: null` behave as expected, not modifying the `Deployment` and leaving `resourceVersion` the same, but empty map `{}` behaves as described above.

If we cannot change this behavior, I'd at least like to understand the rationale behind it.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected my `Deployment` object to stay the same between identical server-side applies, where the manifest file content was exactly the same, regardless of the value of `spec.template.metadata.annotations`. A different `resourceVersion` every apply indicates that the obje
ROOT CAUSE: The server-side apply mechanism treats empty maps (`{}`) as different from nil or absent maps in the live object, causing repeated modifications with no semantic change. This happens because empty maps are not normalized to nil before comparison, leading the apply process to think there is a change and updating the resourceVersion.
FIX: Fix bug where Server Side Apply causing spurious resourceVersion bumps on no-op patches containing empty maps.
